speechtext:
1.	(a) Did the member for Quebec West bring to the attention of the Acting Postmaster General alleged irregularities in the Post Office Department? (b) If so, on what dates?
2.	(a) Did an investigator of the Post Office Department accompany one Marcel Belair to Seven Islands? (b) If so, for what purpose?
3.	Did either of the two thieves convicted in connection with theft at the Cabano post office in the fall of 1953 implicate Belair in any way?
4.	(a) Did one Marcel Belair turn over to postal officials $28,000 worth of stamps stolen from the Notre Dame de Grace post office in February, 1954? (b) If so, under what circumstances? (c) were charges laid? (d) If not, for what reason?
5.	Has the acting postmaster general any further information regarding the alleged irregularities in the Post Office Department, brought to his attention by the member for Quebec West?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question calls for an oral answer. Part 1 of the question reads:
1. (a) Did the member for Quebec West bring to the attention of the Acting Postmaster General alleged irregularities in the Post Office Department? (b) If so, on what dates?
The answer to that question, sir, is as follows: The hon. member for Quebec West stated that several times he had attempted to bring serious irregularities to the attention of the acting postmaster general. The truth is that the only occasion on which the hon. member discussed any alleged irregularities in the Post Office Department with me was about the middle of June, after he had put a series of questions on the order paper about a man named Marcel Belair.
As soon as the answers had been prepared, I asked the hon. member for Quebec West to come to see me in my office where I explained that I felt it would be preferable not to have the answers given in the house because the questions related to a police investigation which had not been completed; and the answers might give information, which they did not already possess, to some of the suspects.
I added, however, that I would give the answers if the hon. member insisted. The hon. member replied that he would like to have the answers put on the record and he added that the information could be of no value to the thieves because this man Belair was no longer at the place where he had been taken by the post office investigators. The hon. member also stated that Belair was being protected by certain investigators of the Post Office Department. I asked him at once if he had given any information he had to the police, or if he would give it to me so that I might have an immediate investigation made. He replied that he had not given the information to the police and declined to give it to me. The hon. member added that he might decide to make accusations in the house but undertook before doing so to advise me. Despite this voluntary promise, I heard nothing more about the matter from the hon. member for Quebec West.
Immediately after this interview, I told the deputy postmaster general what the hon. member had said to me and asked whether the action taken by the postal investigators in arranging employment for Belair at Seven Islands was taken with the knowledge and approval of the police. The deputy minister informed me that the action was taken at the request of the police and that the postal investigators had co-operated throughout with the police. As the hon. member for Quebec West had given me no information on which I could base any further investigation, there was nothing more I could do.
Despite the undertaking he had given me, I was not surprised, however, when I was informed by the press, while I was in Newfoundland, that the hon. member had made certain accusations in the house in my absence from Ottawa.
The second question reads:
2. (a) Did an investigator of the Post Office Department accompany one Marcel Belair to Seven Islands? (b) If so, for what purpose?

Questions
The answer, sir, is as follows: The hon. member for Quebec West stated in the house that an investigator of the Post Office Department accompanied Marcel Belair to Seven Islands for the purpose of hiding him from justice. It is true that an investigator did accompany Belair to Seven Islands and arrange for his employment under an assumed name. I so informed the house on June 20 last in answer to a question by the hon. member for Quebec West.
I have read the report made to the Post Office Department on this incident by the post office investigator, Mr. Fernand Vil-leneuve of Montreal. The report is dated September 22, 1954. According to this report, Belair had been held in custody for some time by the provincial police as a material witness in a case being prepared against another suspected thief. As neither the police nor the department had evidence against Belair on which they felt they were justified in prosecuting, Mr. Justice Wilfrid Lazure, of the court of queen's bench, authorized his release on September 16, 1954. Belair was in custody in Quebec city. Mr. Fernand Villeneuve was instructed to go to Quebec and to arrange for Belair's release with the crown prosecutor's office in Quebec.
On his arrival in Quebec, Mr. Villeneuve got in touch with the crown prosecutor's office and the provincial police and was informed that it had been arranged that Belair would be released and taken to Seven Islands by a member of the provincial police force, who was to arrange for his employment under an assumed name so that he would be available as a witness whenever it might become possible to proceed with the prosecution in which his testimony was required. This arrangement had been agreed to voluntarily by Belair.
Mr. Villeneuve was about to return to Montreal when he was called back to the office of the provincial police and informed that the police felt it would be preferable to have Belair accompanied to Seven Islands by Mr. Villeneuve rather than a provincial policeman. The police provided Mr. Villeneuve with an air ticket and he accompanied Belair to Seven Islands and made arrangements for his employment and for unemployment insurance under the name of Arthur St. Jean. Mr. Villeneuve also bought some work clothes for Belair and gave him $10 to meet his expenses until he began to earn some wages. Before Mr. Villeneuve left Seven Islands, Belair gave his assurance that he would stay there as long as his employer would keep him, but in fact he disappeared a few days later.
Such action had become necessary because of the disappearance of one Lucien Gagnon,
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
now a disbarred Montreal lawyer, who was accused of receiving unemployment insurance stamps stolen from the Ville St. Laurent post office. Belair was a material witness against Gagnon, who, according to the crown prosecutor, had previously succeeded in preventing Belair from giving testimony against him at the preliminary hearing. Belair was taken to Seven Islands with the approval of Mr. Noel Dorion, Q.C., special crown attorney in the case, in order to prevent Gagnon and his friends from subverting Belair again before the trial. I agree with Mr. Dorion that this action was taken in the interests of the proper administration of justice.
That would seem to dispose of the hon. member's accusation that a post office investigator accompanied Marcel Belair to Seven Islands for the purpose of hiding him from justice.
The third question is:
Did either of the two thieves convicted in connection with theft at the Cabano post office in the fall of 1953 implicate Belair in any way?
The answer is:	The hon. member for
Quebec West stated in the house that Belair was never troubled by the police in connection with the burglary at Cabano, although in the written confession made under oath by one of the accused men Belair was implicated in the theft.
The records of the Post Office Department indicate that information was obtained some time in October, 1953, which led to the arrest of two persons suspected of robbing the post office at Cabano on September 16, 1953. Both suspects were questioned at length by the provincial police and by post office investigators. Though the two men pleaded guilty themselves, they did not give the name of any accomplice, and the investigators of the Post Office Department know of no verbal or written statement furnished by either of these suspects which implicated Belair in this burglary. I am informed that, when questioned by Mr. Fortin and Mr. Villeneuve, investigators of the Post Office Department, Belair did say that he knew about the burglary at Cabano but he never admitted having taken part in it and the Post Office Department has never had any evidence of his complicity.
The fourth question is:
(a) Did one Marcel Belair turn over to postal officials $28,000 worth of stamps stolen from the Notre Dame de Grace post office in February, 1954?	(b) If so, under what circumstances?
(c) Were charges laid? (d) If not, for what reason.
The answer is: The hon. member for Quebec West stated that the post office investigators learned that their friend, Belair, was in possession of $28,000 worth of stamps

connection with another robbery. All four made by the police with the full approval of had lengthy police records. The suspects the crown prosecutor in the province of refused to talk and were about to be released Quebec. The fifth question, sir, is:

After some questioning, Belair told Mr. Villeneuve that, if he was released, he would try to recover the postage stamps and unemployment insurance stamps stolen from the Notre Dame de Grace postal station. On this occasion Belair gave Mr. Villeneuve valuable information regarding other post office thefts, which information led to the arrest of Lucien Gagnon, a Montreal barrister, on a charge of receiving stolen goods. Mr. Villeneuve at once informed both the provincial and municipal police of the offer made by Belair to find the stamps and they agreed to release Belair and to keep the other three suspects in custody.
Mr. Villeneuve reports that Belair made no condition except that Mr. Villeneuve should accompany him and that they should not be followed by anyone. They went to an address on St. Denis street in Montreal the first day and waited for some time, but did not get the stamps. Mr. Villeneuve and Belair met again the following day and this time went to Belair's mother's house which Belair entered alone. When he came out he told Mr. Villeneuve to go into the lane and pick up a suitcase and a parcel. These two articles were taken by Mr. Villeneuve to Mr. Fortin and other officials. On investigation, it was found that the parcel contained $1,900 worth of stamps and the suitcase contained some torches.
Both the provincial and the municipal police were notified at once. Mr. Villeneuve got in touch with Belair again and told him what he had found in the suitcase. Belair appeared surprised and said there must have been a mistake and promised to get the stamps the next day. The following day Mr. Villeneuve accompanied Belair to a private house in the north end of the city. They went into a front room and Belair told Mr. Villeneuve to open a valise they found there. The valise was full of stamps. The recovery of the stamps was at once reported to Mr. Fortin and to the provincial and municipal police.
Belair never at any time admitted taking part in the Notre Dame de Grace robbery.
Has the Acting Postmaster General any further information regarding the alleged irregularities in the Post Office Department, brought to his attention by the member for Quebec West?
The answer, sir, is: As soon as I returned from Newfoundland on Thursday evening, July 21, I got in touch with the deputy postmaster general, who had already arranged to have Mr. Villeneuve, one of the investigators of the Post Office Department, as well as other postal officials available to meet me. The deputy minister informed me that Mr. Villeneuve had reported to the department on the evening of July 18 concerning an interview he had had with one Gerard Gagnon, of Quebec, who had informed Mr. Villeneuve that certain accusations were going to be made in the House of Commons the next day. This information was passed on to the deputy minister who instructed Mr. Villeneuve to make a sworn statement of what had taken place in this interview. In view of the character of this statement, I shall not attempt to paraphrase it but shall read it exactly as it was handed to me by Mr. Villeneuve on Thursday evening.
The sworn statement reads as follows:
I, Fernand Villeneuve, of 11805 Filion street, Ville St-Laurent, in the county of Montreal 9, province of Quebec, do solemnly declare that
In the forenoon of July 19, Miss Thibault of the office of the regional director, phoned me concerning a telephone call she had received from a Mr. Gerard Gagnon of Quebec city who wanted to speak to Mr. Fortin for a very important matter and when told that Mr. Fortin was out of town, he asked to speak to me. Miss Thibault gave him my phone number and Mr. Gagnon called me around 11 a.m. on July 19, 1955.
Mr. Gagnon made an appointment to meet me at the office of the investigations division on the same day around 3 p.m. He said that it was something very important.
He did not come at the time expected and around 4 p.m. he called me, excused himself and asked me at what time I could see him. 1 told him that I was at his disposition even after the office hours. He then said that it was preferable that I see him at his room in view of the nature of the case he had to discuss with me.
I made arrangements to meet him at his room No. 581 at the Queen's hotel.
In view of the fact that he had asked to speak to Mr. Fortin and then to myself, I suspected that it was concerning Lucien Gagnon and before going to his room, I went to check with the house officer of the Queen's hotel, the records of room 581.

Questions
The records showed that Mr. and Mrs. Gerard Gagnon of Quebec city had registered on that day. To the records was attached a business card of Gagnon Transport Limitee of Quebec and Montreal.
Gerard Gagnon did not arrive until 6 p.m. When I went in, his wife was on the phone and he told me that he would wait until she was finished as he wanted to be alone to discuss what he had to say.
While his wife was on the phone, he showed me a piece of paper on which were different remarks concerning Lucien Gagnon and Marcel Belair. He took this paper back but from what I can recollect, the remarks were something as follows: "Lucien Gagnon is staying in New York city. Marcel Belair is also in the states and he would have lately been suspected of having taken part in a burglary. Marcel Belair had registered at Seven Islands under a false name. A postal investigator paid with his personal cheque goods purchased for Belair. A postal investigator connected with Marcel Belair has been promoted."
Mr. Gerard Gagnon then asked his wife to leave which she did, and after her departure, Mr. Gagnon told me "You know now what I wanted to see you for?" I answered in the affirmative. He first began to tell me that he was not related in any way to Lucien Gagnon and that he was not a friend of him but he was interested concerning a very important transaction involving over $100,000 and that in order to have this transaction go through, it would be necessary to have Lucien Gagnon in Montreal, that this could not be done if Lucien Gagnon was behind the bars. He then asked me if it would be possible for Lucien Gagnon to obtain bail should he present himself. I told Mr. Gerard Gagnon that it was up to the department of the attorney general to decide. Mr. Gagnon then said that the attorney general would need the consent of post office officials since the charge had been laid by post office investigators.
Mr. Gerard Gagnon was told that as far as I was concerned, I could not give my consent. Mr. Gagnon then repeated that he was not interested about the case of Lucien Gagnon but only concerning the transaction and added he saw no reason why I would not give my consent. I then told him that I would contact the authorities but that I doubted very much if they would give their approbation.
I related to Mr. Gerard Gagnon what Judge Lazure had said when one of the lawyers of Lucien Gagnon had made a request for bail. Judge Lazure had then informed that he would not grant bail even if they would offer one for a million dollars.
Mr. Gagnon then told me that serious accusations would be made in the House of Commons, very y the following day concerning Fortin and Villeneuve that a member of parliament had a number of affidavits signed by Marcel Belair and others and that mention would be made concerning promotion of a high official who had been closely connected with this case. I cannot of course remember all what Mr. Gagnon said, but he did make allusion of an officer having been seen often in a night club with Marcel Belair and that the same officer was the owner of a bad house where post office officials used to meet.
I told Mr. Gagnon that I was perfectly at ease and that everything that was done concerning this case was in the interest of justice and that we had nothing to hide.
Mr. Gagnon then said that even if what will be said against Fortin and myself is not all true, there is always something left and that it would of course be preferable not to have anything of the kind mentioned.
tMr. Pickersgill.]
Gerard Gagnon then spoke again of Lucien Gagnon and told me that he knew he was in New York and added that he would see lawyer Noel Dorion, Q.C. crown prosecutor in this case and he then asked me to take the matter over. I told him that if I could contact the authorities, particularly Mr. Fortin, I would call him up.
Around noon on July 20th, I tried to reach him (G. Gagnon) to advise him that I would not be able to see Mr. Fortin before the end of the week, but could not contact him.
I have not heard from Gerard Gagnon since.
The same evening, that is, July 19th, I informed Mr. Pageau-
Who is an official of the Post Office Department, I might interject.
-who is presently in Montreal, of the result of the interview I had with Mr. Gerard Gagnon, and after having discussed the case over again, the following morning, it was then agreed to inform the deputy postmaster general which was done at 12 p.m. by Mr. Pageau in my presence.
I had never met nor heard of this Gerard Gagnon before and found very strange, the request he made and all he had told me about the accusations that were to be made.
AND I MAKE this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true, and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
DECLARED before me at Montreal in the county of in the province of Quebec
this 21st day of July, 1955


f (Sgd.) Fernand Villeneuve

As I told the house, I immediately asked the deputy postmaster general whether everything that had been done in connection with this Belair affair had been done with the knowledge and approval of the police, and I was assured that it had been done not only with their knowledge and approval but in some cases at the instance of the police and with the full knowledge and approval of Mr. Noel Dorion, Q.C., who is the special crown prosecutor in these cases. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 20 I asked the Acting Postmaster General certain questions. Question No. 3 was:
Was the said investigator following instructions of the department and acting on its behalf on this trip?
The answer is "Yes". Question No. 4 was:
If so. what were the reasons for this trip and what was accomplished by the said investigator?
The answer was as follows:
The trip was made in connection with a police investigation which is still in progress.
From the investigator's report can the minister tell me how many persons were questioned in Seven Islands on that trip regarding this police investigation about which he has talked?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It must be quite obvious that no persons were questioned in Seven Islands in connection with this police investigation. It is perfectly obvious from the statement I made to the house that the police investigation was taking place largely in Montreal, and that the purpose of taking this man, Belair, to Seven Islands and securing employment for him there was to provide him with an honest means of livelihood so that he would not be dependent-

maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: -upon the gang with which it was suspected he was associated, the gang of this disbarred lawyer, Gagnon, and so that he would be available when required as a witness in the case if Gagnon's case could be brought before the courts. That is the police investigation I was referring to, the investigation of Gagnon.

maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Could the minister tell me where the written confession is which was given to the investigators regarding the Cabano theft and which was written by one Germain Dumont?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Could the minister explain how Belair could know who the post office investigators were in order to approach them if he were not in some way closely connected with them? I understand there is no answer to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: How many interviews has the acting minister or the deputy postmaster general had since my speech in the house last Wednesday, July 20, with the two investigators mentioned and probably also with Marcel Belair?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I do not think, strictly speaking, that I should answer that question at all. I am charged with the responsibility temporarily, and I must say I hope it will be very temporary, of administering the department. While I am charged with the responsibility I am responsible for what goes on and the number of times I see officials is, I think, a private matter within my jurisdiction. But I do not mind answering the question. I saw Mr. Villeneuve on Thursday evening. I saw Mr. Villeneuve again on Friday. I saw Mr. Villeneuve and Mr. Fortin on Saturday and I saw both of them for about one minute this morning. As for Belair, to the best of my knowledge and belief I have never seen him in my life. Mr. Gerard Gagnon, who seems to be very well known to the hon. member, says he is in the United States.

If he and the police are not able to furnish a satisfactory explanation of the matter it will, of course, be investigated further. I took, out of the mixture of fact and innuendo, to which the house was treated the other day by the hon. member, all the alleged facts, and I asked questions about them of the officials. I had verified with the crown prosecutor, all the facts or alleged facts that the hon. gentleman had in his statement, and it is apparent that none of these alleged facts is, in fact, correct.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Without in any way enlarging upon the rather ingenious explanation of some remarkably irregular practices which has been given by the minister, might I ask him if he proposes to do anything about the statement made by the deputy postmaster general to the Ottawa Citizen and reported in its issue of July 22? I refer him to his statement:
Admitting that he was far from satisfied with the number of prosecutions in connection with post office robberies, he laid the full responsibility for this situation on the shoulders of local police authorities.
"It is significant", he said, "that although 22 post office robberies occurred in Vancouver and New Westminster since January 1, 1953, in not one case have the police apprehended the criminals."

Questions
Does the minister not think the statement of the deputy postmaster general, quite regardless of his interpretation of the particular case under discussion, merits examination and investigation to ascertain where the trouble lies? If it is outside the department, well and good; but on the statement of the deputy postmaster general there is a situation where no prosecutions have been registered in connection with 22 known cases of theft.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I said the other day that I thought it was rather unfortunate that any statement or any answers to questions-because this is not a statement by the deputy postmaster general-had been made. He was asked by an individual newspaperman who took this return, of which I have a copy, the return that was made at the time the Post Office Department estimates were up, and asked a number of questions about these specific thefts. The deputy postmaster general gave some answers.
Now, the fact is, as I think all members of the house, and certainly all members of the bar, must realize, that post office investigators are not policemen; they are not prosecutors. They are investigators, and they can only go to a certain stage and then lay an information. From then on, the matter has to be followed up by the police. To the best of my knowledge the police follow these things up as best they can. As I said when the post office estimates were before the house, it is often very difficult to find someone to arrest and to get enough evidence on which to base a charge. The Post Office Department does its utmost, through its investigators, to get all the evidence it can to assist the police. But, as everyone knows, the responsibility for apprehending criminals and for bringing them to justice is the responsibility of the attorney general in each of the provinces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I have no desire to pursue this unnecessarily, and I want to make it quite clear that I have no knowledge of any of the facts that have been previously discussed. I am merely relating my remarks to the statements of the deputy postmaster general following what I have already quoted, and this is a direct quotation:
"We are at the mercy of the police in every community," he added. "In any community where a series of post office thefts have occurred without subsequent successful action on the part of the police authorities it is a reflection on the police force of those communities."
I ask, Mr. Speaker, whether, in the face of that statement by the deputy postmaster general, which is not challenged so far as accuracy is concerned, there is no ground

for investigation. An investigation would fulfil the very purpose he has himself indicated of clearing the officials referred to of any implication, and of ascertaining where there is a breakdown in the administration of justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I did not submit the deputy postmaster general to a detailed catechism on this press report. If he said those words in the way in which they appear there, and it is possible he did, it is unfortunate. I do not think any of us here want to reflect upon police forces that are under jurisdictions other than our own. Certainly I do not. And I think it is much more likely that he used the phrase "at the mercy of" in a rather loose sense, meaning that it was the responsibility of the police.
Now, that is correct; it is the responsibility of the police. It is the responsibility and duty of the Post Office Department to do its utmost to assist. But it is the responsibility of the police, if they can find them, to arrest criminals and bring them to justice. My knowledge of these matters is very, very limited indeed; but from what I have already discovered in this brief time in connection with this Belair case, it does seem to me there has been most excellent co-operation between the Post Office Department, and the attorney general's department, and the crown prosecutor, and the provincial police of the province of Quebec in this particular case. And, as I say, that is the one that is under review. That is the one about which I had attempted, as far as I could, to ascertain the facts.
About what the situation may be in Vancouver, I have not felt it was my duty as acting minister to investigate that particularly; but if the hon. member would like me to, I can make some inquiry about it. But I would imagine that the police in Vancouver, or in British Columbia generally, are just as anxious to bring these criminals to justice as the police in any other part of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: *POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I will close with these remarks: I would point out that I did not raise this. I am simply pointing out that the deputy postmaster general voluntarily, in his discussion of another subject in another province, raised this question of 22 known robberies in Vancouver and New Westminster in regard to which there had been no one apprehended. It does seem to me that this calls for some consideration by the minister. This is not something I am putting forward, but something I have read in a press statement, which is not challenged by the deputy postmaster general, and which is reported by a very responsible reporter who speaks in exact quotes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in this group are very much concerned with the amendment and, on that account, on behalf of this group I wish to say a few words about it. In our opinion the adoption of this amendment would mean the destruction of the annuities act and a breach of faith on the part of this parliament with those who have invested their hard-earned savings in annuities to provide income in their declining years. We most strongly oppose this deification of the cash register as against our acceptance of social responsibility for human needs and welfare, and a recognition of contracts entered into by thousands of people in good faith.
In our opinion this motion is spawned from an economic philosophy that would have denied British financial aid in her hour of need and greatly reduced Canadian markets for grain, on that account; would have undermined our universal old age security system; would have liquidated our agricultural support prices policy and, to some extent, ruined the dairy farmers of Canada; would have left unsheltered any poverty-stricken Indian without the means to build a home; would have left untaxed the excess profits of the larger corporations in this country. It would also mean that we should defer the value of an investment by the people of Canada in a national library. The same philosophy would leave other countries uninformed about Canadian activities, by the dissolution of the international service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It would begrudge our civil servants an adequate reserve for their superannuation fund. Also

it opposes freight assistance on western feed grains required by the farmers of British Columbia and eastern Canada, if they are to continue to produce dairy, beef and poultry products without loss. It would deny to the Quebec maple syrup producers the purchase of aluminum pails so as to prevent any possibility of lead poisoning of consumers in Canada.
In our opinion the text of the advocates of this economic philosophy is: Save the taxpayers' money. We in this group are in favour of economy and efficient administration; but what these people really mean when they say "Save the taxpayers' money" is "Save the big taxpayers' money".
I would remind the house that this was the favourite slogan of the former President Hoover of the United States, who sat with palsied financial hands for two or three years while millions went hungry in the United States, and until the late President Roosevelt remedied the situation. This was a favourite phrase, you will find if you read parliamentary records, of the Chamberlain family in Great Britain, whose economic and other policies brought such suffering to the workers in that country.
In our opinion this is the economic philosophy of some people on Bay street and St. James street. But, fortunately, the philosophy that prompts this amendment is not the philosophy of progressive capitalists. I think we must give them credit for believing in periodic inoculations of relative economic and social justice in order to defeat the virus of totalitarianism.
This resolution springs from the extreme right in economic thinking. We in this group believe that instead of limiting this form of insurance-and it is a form of insurance- we should be evolving a scheme on a wider basis to cover the whole population. And this idea has been expressed in the house on many occasions.
On February 12, 1934, William Irvine moved the following resolution:
That in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the advisability of nationalizing life insurance.
In reading the record I find that during the debate the resolution was supported by the present Senator Howden, and several other Liberal speakers. When the vote was taken, it was interesting to note it was supported by that great Canadian whom we all respect, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley. The hon. member for Cape Breton South and other members have urged a system of national industrial pensions. This question has been discussed at length in the British

house on occasion. Even the Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill, when speaking on this question, had this to say:
You must rank me and my colleagues as strong partisans of national compulsory insurance, for all purposes, from the cradle to the grave. We hope to bring the magic of averages to the rescue of millions.
I just want to say on behalf of this group, Mr. Chairman, this is a great question that must receive careful consideration by this house in the near future. Today there are millions in Canada lacking the opportunity to provide further for their old age at cost. Today there are thousands in Canada lacking satisfactory homes and accommodation. Today insurance companies with vast investments refuse to expand their investments in this field, and on that account it was necessary for the government to provide for the banks to make loans for housing.
In my opinion, through an over-all national insurance scheme, we can provide a measure of security for all our citizens and considerable funds that can be used in a public investment program for houses, for highways and for public facilities, and so on.
We trust-and when I say "we" I mean members of this group for whom I am speaking this morning on this question-that, by unanimous defeat of this motion, this house will allay the fears of those who are on old age security, old age assistance, disability pensions, war veterans allowance, family allowances, civil service superannuation and annuities; that this parliament would even consider the reduction of these benefits to save the taxpayers' money. This suggestion, that we suffer from a leprosy of the human spirit as indicated in this motion, must be cured, in the opinion of this group, by unanimous disapproval of this motion.

It would be wholly impossible for the government, through the annuities branch, to carry out its obligations under the annuity contracts which have already been entered into, and I call upon the committee to reject this motion promptly.
The hon. gentleman who proposed it said that the cost of each contract to the taxpayer was roughly $54. interest involved, this is legislation to which the government attaches great importance and value. I hope the motion will be speedily defeated.

speechtext: I should like to ask the Acting Minister of Labour two or three questions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I shall try to accommodate the minister in that respect. I think my first question will be quite easy to answer. Has the Canadian government any regulation restricting United States labour coming to Canada to work?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, there is a free movement between the two countries which of course is subject to the immigration laws. For instance, there are a great number of Canadians living in my own community who work in Detroit and I sincerely hope that nothing will happen-some consideration is now being given in the United States to this matter-to prevent those citizens continuing to work in Detroit. While the number is smaller, there are some United States citizens who work in our city and the same is true of all border points generally. Subject to our immigration and wage laws there is no fundamental restriction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Are there any United States restrictions preventing certain classes of Canadian labour working in the United States?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Yes, there are.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Could the minister tell us what they are?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I do not think I can give all the details. First of all, I do know that people who are guilty of a crime of moral turpitude cannot get into that country, and there are certain other prohibited classes. As I said a moment ago, a committee in the United States is investigating this matter and I saw that it was sitting in Detroit the other day. At one time you could not take a job in the United States unless you had in being certain funds of your own or unless you intended to establish a business which you would conduct yourself or which would necessitate hiring help. There are some restrictions but I just cannot give all the classifications.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: What I had in mind particularly was construction labour or construction superintendents coming to Canada from the United States to work on construction jobs in this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: That is a matter for immigration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Apparently the United States government is conducting some sort of investigation into Canadians working in the United States, and I would refer to an article in the Windsor Star of Saturday, July 16, with which the minister no doubt is familiar. That being so, possibly the Canadian government, the Department of Labour particularly, might consider investigating the same thing on this side of the line. It is my understanding that there are a good many United States companies, particularly construction companies, who set up subsidiary companies in Canada and then bring in United States labour, particularly managerial and supervisory staffs, foremen and that type of thing. This is particularly the case in southern Ontario, but my understanding is that it is happening in Milton, Toronto, Hamilton and other places. My suggestion is that the Canadian government should investigate this matter because there is plenty of the same type of labour available in Canada. This was particularly so last winter. I am quite aware that the unemployment situation has decreased considerably, but during the winter and fall and spring jobs are likely to be scarce and this practice makes it that much harder for Canadian labour to obtain employment. I am not suggesting that the government should start anything that might lead to acrimonious exchanges from both sides of the border,
Supply-Labour
but if the United States government is carrying on such an investigation it seems to me that the Canadian government might well look into this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I think my hon. friend and the government are fully in accord on this matter. As I indicated the other day and a few minutes ago, we are aware of the studies that are being made in the United States, but it is not desirable to create animosity between the two countries when we get along so well. Where a construction company wants to come into Canada to carry on a project we do not permit them to bring in a full labour force, apart from key personnel such as executive and managerial people, if Canadian labour is available. The department of immigration would work through the Department of Labour and we are actually carrying on the very practice to which my hon. friend asks us to give some study.

speechtext:
There is another matter which I think could be raised under this vote. There is another angle about which I should like to ask the minister. It does not concern people coming in from the United States to work as superintendents or foremen on special jobs, and there is a great deal of that in British Columbia. What I have in mind, and I presume it comes under the same discussion, is that people have come into Canada, particularly western Canada, in great numbers over the past two years, not as foremen or superintendents, but actually as salesmen.
I am glad that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is sitting alongside the minister now. They actually come in as visitors and for periods of from two weeks to two months carry out high pressure sales campaigns for roofing, stucco and things of that nature.
As soon as we draw this matter to the attention of the Department of Labour or the department of immigration, they step in and tell them to get out of British Columbia, but two or three weeks later we find they are coming into Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba and doing the same thing. I know it has done a great deal of harm to established business in the province of British Columbia and I know it has ruined many people because they have lost hundreds or thousands of dollars through this high pressure business. Is that the responsibility of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or does it come under the Department of Labour? No matter whom it comes under, can there not be more investigation and a closer check held on these people who are pulling these stunts in Canada?

course, each country establishes its own wage scales, and that is the situation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I should like to suggest to the Acting Minister of Labour that under this item he investigate one of the other departments, namely, that of the Secretary of State, in connection with the civil service.
I find that this legislation dates back to 1900, when parliament passed a resolution outlining the ideas regarding a fair wage policy but, coming up to date, in 1953 P.C. 4138

became effective, which has a clause prohibiting discrimination in employment because of race, national origin, colour, religion or because the employee has made a complaint or given information with respect to such discrimination. I find that the civil service commission-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: This does not come under this item. It is strictly out of order. I suggest the hon. member bring it up under item No. 178.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: In view of the minister's reply, I should like to ask this question. I know this is not regularly the minister's department, but does he not think he can do anything about this practice? Does he believe that having one employee receiving one wage and another employee receiving another wage working at the same time would lead to anything but discontent on the part of labour working under such conditions? It seems most unfair to me. I know, for instance, if I were working on the St. Lawrence seaway for $1.50 an hour and an American next to me doing the same job was getting $1.75 or $2 an hour, I would certainly resent it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: If it happens to be a United States contractor and the work is wholly performed in Canada, he must, of course, conform to the Canadian wage laws.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Then, from what the acting minister says, it is not a fact that if Americans are brought over to do labour in Canada on these construction jobs they receive more than Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: It must be done according to Canadian law.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I am informed from several sources that is not the case. Americans coming over here get more money than Canadians for the same work.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: They may receive more, but the wage at least must meet Canadian minimum wage standards.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I should like to ask the acting minister whether under this section any research is being done in connection with finding a solution to labour disputes in the field of public utilities? I think there is growing across Canada a conviction in the minds of the population as a whole that we have to find a better way of settling labour disputes in the field of public utilities. I know this is also shared by a great number of workers in the public utilities themselves.
I know this may possibly affect more the provincial departments of labour, but the federal government is also involved in the operation of public utilities. For instance,
I should very much like to see the federal

government take the lead in doing some research in perhaps finding out what other means would be acceptable to labour. I know that labour very tenaciously, and I think rightfully, clings to the right to strike, even in public utilities. However, labour itself in a number of those fields recognizes that it is an inhumane and almost impossible thing to do. Hospital employees will suffer a great deal of discrimination and what they may consider substandard working conditions and wages in order to keep the hospitals in operation, and so on.
I note that this section of the department takes up almost half a million dollars. I wonder whether any of that $471,000 is being spent in the field of exploring the possibilities of a new way out in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: There is provision made for grants to several universities which are engaged in trying to find more satisfactory techniques not only in the field of public utilities but in other fields as well. I have in mind particularly the work being done in the department of economics, Queen's University, under Professor Cameron, some work being done at Toronto and in British Columbia. Therefore my hon. friend may be assured that not only tentative but active consideration is being given to this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Did I hear the minister say that part of this allotment was to be used to provide such grants?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: It is paid under another vote, the economics branch. It is vote No. 174.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
There is a problem I should like to discuss at this time. I have one of the announcements of the civil service commission of Canada before me, and quite a number of similar announcements have come in the mail recently. In part it has this to say:
Married women may apply, but will be listed for temporary appointment only unless they can satisfy the commission that they are required to be self-supporting. An affidavit to this effect must accompany the application.
I can understand that when this legislation was originally passed in 1900 the Victorian thinking of the era might require this sort of regulation, but surely in the year 1955 we should not be stipulating that while there must be no discrimination regarding race, national origin, colour or religion there may be discrimination regarding sex. I am sure all members will agree that woman's finest contribution is probably in the home, but in this day and age, with the electrical gadgets
Supply-Labour
they have in their kitchens, I think the government should not be the organization to say that no married woman will be permitted to work unless she makes such an affidavit. The language used in the announcement is:
Married women may apply, but will be listed for temporary appointment only unless they can satisfy the commission that they are required to be self-supporting.
Surely people do not work just for the sake of working. Anyone who works wants to do something with the pay cheque received every week, twice a month or once a month. People are paying for their homes. Certainly in this country you cannot live in the open in the wintertime. You must have some shelter, and the providing of shelter is beyond the means of a great many of the wage earners of Canada. If there is to be decent shelter, then in all probability the wife has to do some work. Would the minister indicate if he does not think that action should be taken against his colleague, the Secretary of State, who is responsible for the civil service commission, to see if something cannot be done regarding the discriminatory provision now found in most of the notices being issued in connection with appointments?
There are a great many capable women in the civil service. Does this mean that if these women decide to marry they will not be permitted to carry on their employment? Surely it should be recognized that the more people who do useful work in Canada the higher standard of living we will all enjoy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I will be very glad to see that the Secretary of State and I have an opportunity to discuss this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I think the Acting Minister of Labour should go further. I think he should have some opinion to express.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: The Acting Minister of Labour will express no opinion until he has had a chance to pursue the matter further with his colleague.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Can the minister give us an idea of how many people received assistance or training under this scheme last year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, this is a very important phase of the over-all problem of rehabilitation which arises out of the decision made by the federal government and the provinces three years ago, and it fits very much into the plans that we have very actively under way in the Department of National Health and Welfare. At the end of June there were applications for service from 1,554 cases. Service has been provided to 1,096, and about 300 had been rehabilitated.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Because of the remarks made by the hon. member for Charlotte on Saturday, I should like to point out to the minister that this item calls for an appropriation of $201,000. Last year the estimate was $197,000. The actual expenditure last year was $92,637, about half the amount of the appropriation. Now you are appropriating about $4,000 more. Would it not be more in keeping with economy if you would pare down the amount to about $100,000, because that is all that would appear to be required? It was said

that we in the official opposition are not on the job in checking up these things, and I should like to know why you have so large an estimate here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Agreements have only been signed recently with the provinces, and there are a number of co-ordinators to be appointed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Is there any reason why you are going to spend more money this year than you have in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR

To provide for carrying out the purposes of the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act and agreements made thereunder: to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with any province on terms approved by the governor in council to provide financial assistance to vocational schools, and training under youth training projects and to provide for the expenditures thereunder and under vocational training agreements entered into in previous years-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I would not want to tie up the acting minister under any circumstances, but I have a few words to say about item 184.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: The acting minister will do his best to get untied.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: It has to do with vocational training. In the part of the country from which I come, it is a very important subject. I notice the estimates this year-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I appreciate that fact, too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I know you do. The grants to the provinces are down this year by $109,500, and the grants for capital expenditures, that is to assist in building schools, are down by more than $200,000. I have always held the opinion that the trend should be in the opposite direction. Now, I am not going into a long harangue on the matter, as I have done a good many times. But I would suggest to the minister and to his department that something is needed in the part of the country from which I come, Cape Breton island, along the lines of vocational training and, at this time, I believe the retraining of people who are being rooted out of the mining industry.
For many years we have been trying to establish on that island a trade training

school. It is something that is badly needed. The island is the biggest industrial centre east of Montreal, and has no vocational training facilities at this time. In the past, the difficulty has been in raising the necessary money to build a proper school. Despite promises by the provincial government in at least four provincial elections that the school was going to be undertaken, nothing has been done. I know the federal minister of labour and his officials have in the past tried, without success, to get an agreement on the matter of erecting a school, and then maintaining it afterwards. Some of the municipalities involved found it difficult to raise their share of the funds.
I would suggest to the minister that there is only about 40 per cent of our school population that go through high school, and there is only about 10 per cent that get to university. This means that 90 per cent of our school population is leaving school each year and going into the labour market without any training of any kind. It is nearly time we did something about it. If the national average for students getting through university is 10 per cent, then in the part of the country from which I come it is much lower. The only thing we have had to export during the last 20 years has been our young people. The least we can do for them, after putting them through high school or as far as they can get because of economic and other circumstances, is to give them training in a trade so that when they move out they have something to sell.
There are thousands of miners rooted out of the coal industry during the past three or four years-800 more a few days ago- who will have to move out. Instead of letting them sit down and draw unemployment insurance for a year or more until it runs out, proper facilities should be provided now to retrain them in some other kind of employment. It always looked rather ridiculous to me to find that year after year we are bringing immigrants here and placing them in various sections of Canada, while we have a section like that in which the people could be truly classified as displaced persons. These people have been uprooted, and they will have to move out. There should be some kind of organization on the part of the provincial and federal governments to see to it that these people are not only able to maintain themselves but are able to make their maximum contribution to our economy. There has not been enough done about it.
I know the minister has a broad social outlook and he made a recent visit to that
Supply-Labour
part of the country. He was very well received, and I have had a lot of commendation since-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Thanks to your hospitality
and that of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria; you were both very generous hosts.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I am sure we all benefited from the visit. I am just leaving these few thoughts with the minister. I could talk for an hour on this subject. I have discussed this matter with the Minister of Labour personally, and perhaps the acting minister can get together with him to see if something cannot be done about getting a trade school for that area, not only for the purpose of training these boys and girls who may make use of it in the future but for the purpose of retraining these men today who take a very dim view of life because they have lost their employment overnight. I leave these thoughts with the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I know the Minister of Labour is very interested in this matter. He asked me to assure my hon. friend of his deep interest in this problem. I can say with regard to the proposed provincial school that the federal government now stands ready, as it has before, to put up its share towards this particular school when the other governmental authority sees fit to put forward a proposition. I think we can sympathize with what the hon. gentleman has said about the closing of the mine, particularly that of the other day leaving some 700 individuals out of work. While there may be discussions going on now as to their contract position in terms of priority within the company as a whole, that does not alter the fact that there is a great advantage in this vocational training. I will certainly see to it that the Minister of Labour has an opportunity of reading the very sound observations made by the gentleman who has just spoken.
The government has not reduced this vote. It does appear in the estimates as though the vote actually had been reduced, but it only represents a reduction from expenditures provided for last year which included a grant of $350,000 for the Canadian National Institute for the Blind building in Toronto and $200,000 which represents a capital expenditure on vocational schools which have been completed. Since 1945 the government has paid something like $43 million, I think, for vocational training. There is now an annual appropriation of about $2 million. It is intended that this appropriation should go on for this year. There was no long-term contract made. We are meeting with the provinces in October, as my hon. friend knows, when the long-term aspects of this policy

Supply-Labour
will be reviewed and discussed. My hon. friend knows that the amount which is made available to us in Nova Scotia is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $300,000 out of this $2 million.
I thank my hon. friend for bringing this to our attention, and I assure him it will receive the most sympathetic attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I very briefly want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South because I have discussed the matter with a great number of people in British Columbia. There is some interest in this question, and the more you travel around Canada the more you find there is an unfilled need for skilled artisans, and at the same time we have these unemployed Canadian citizens of Nova Scotia. It is obvious that with the present construction program in industrial plants, in homes, building of highways and other things, there is going to be an increasing demand for skilled workers. I think this vocational training, and this construction program, provide an opportunity for a number of trained workers, and for those who have to be retrained. As I understand it, we might consider this item as the counterpart of university grants to look after these young men particularly, who are not able to take advantage of academic training. In my opinion our expanding economy, and the numbers involved who are untrained at this time, warrant an increase in this vote.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I rise to support what has been said by the member for Cape Breton South in this connection. If I may say so, without being out of order, the time has come when the dominion's appropriations to the maritime provinces should be based on something more than just population, and the income those provinces are able to get from their economies. Surely when any province entered confederation it received the right to participate on equal terms in the good things Canadians as a whole can produce. In effect, that right is denied the maritimes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I should interrupt to say that when I said $30 million I should have said $43 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Well, even at $43 million, the position remains the same.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I just wished to correct the record-because the hon. member suggests some good ideas, and I always listen to him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: How much of that goes to Nova Scotia? Is it just $300,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
The total was $43 million and the annual appropriation is $2 million, of which $300,000 goes to Nova Scotia. It is on a per capita basis. The hon. member is now

arguing the question of need, a very important question; and I know that when the dominion-provincial conference takes place that matter will receive attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I hope it receives effective attention.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I shall do my best, as the hon. member knows.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: The effective right to participate in the great volume of good things Canadians can produce is denied the maritime provinces, because under circumstances restricting them at present their capacity for industrial development is meagre. Consequently they cannot in any way substantially increase their population. This means that they have to go on being poor relations to the other provinces-and that is just not good enough. So I would say that much more generous goals should be kept in mind by the central authorities in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: We may even give consideration to taking something away from some of the wealthier provinces-for instance, in view of the high revenues in Alberta, it might be possible there-and we might give some to the maritime provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Let me tell the minister how he can do that. Let me tell him exactly how he can do it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate that I was just trying to help him along-and I know he is going to help me along.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I am sure of that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I am glad.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: The minister helped me along in what he said. Now, if we had an instrument like the finance act of 1914, and under that finance act we created $500,000 right here in Ottawa, and put that $500,000 into the hands of Nova Scotians, we would with our present great surplus production not take a single cent away from any other province in Canada, but at the same time we would permit Nova Scotia to buy $500,000 worth of goods produced anywhere in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I was not making the suggestion; I was just raising a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Order. May I draw to the attention of the Acting Minister of Labour and the hon. member for Lethbridge that at the moment we are not discussing the principle of grants to provinces, but rather the advisability of voting $75,000 for the

purpose of vocational training. I would ask both hon. members to restrict their remarks to vocational training.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: We thank you, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: You seem to be terribly quick on the trigger. You do not let me get down to what I want to say before you stop me. But the important thing is this, that that $500,000 of created money could be used for vocational training-and I just wish to make that clear to the minister. We should not start taking moneys collected in taxation by or from the wealthier provinces, because that would be unfair to their people. But certainly it is grossly unfair to Nova Scotia, and to any of the other maritime provinces, to receive only the meagre pittance we offer them in respect of practically every single grant that goes from Ottawa to those provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some months ago I asked the Minister of Labour about the future of vocational training. I had a very good reason for asking, because two provincial ministers of education had expressed some concern. They were afraid that the federal department of labour might be contemplating withdrawing from the field of vocational training. In reply to my question the minister said, in effect-and I wish to be fair to him-that the reason the 10-year agreement had not been renewed, and had been replaced by one-year agreements, was that he was planning this conference with the provinces; and the acting minister now says that the conference will be held in October.
I am very pleased that this meeeting is to be held. However, at this time I wish the acting minister would state in no unmistakable terms that it is the intention of the federal government to continue to take a most active, and even a more active, part in the whole matter of aid for educational training.
The reason I appeal to the acting minister to make public some such announcement at this time, long before the October conference-although it is only three months away now-is that in this field of providing educational facilities you cannot plan on a year-to-year basis. The educational authorities back home need more assurance than that, and they are seriously handicapped when they find out that the new agreement will last for only one year, subject to a complete review of the whole situation.
I endorse what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and I would also like to add that the whole problem is
Supply-Labour
growing rapidly in intensity, not only because of the many thousands who are displaced by the complete collapse of certain industrial areas in Canada, but also because of the extension of the age to which people are able to live. We have more older people now than we had some years ago. I find in my riding a growing number of people around the age of 42 or 43 years who, very profitably, could get a good deal of help and a new lease on life if they were able to take advantage of vocational training. This is a matter that will have growing national importance and I appeal to the minister, if he is able, to commit the government at least to the principle of continued participation on a scale not less than has been the case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I cannot say any more than I have said. The matter will be discussed with the provinces, and they have been so advised. We have renewed the agreement for one year. The hon. member cannot expect me to go further than that at this stage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: That just adds a little more ammunition to the growing suspicion throughout Canada that this federal government is planning deliberately to get out from under.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I assure the hon. member there is no justification for that statement. But it would be wrong for any member of the government to go to a conference, after having prejudged the issue. I have indicated our interest. We are going to discuss these serious matters, and the provinces have been so advised. But they would not expect us to say any more than I have said here today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: One o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Can we not pass this item?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: Does not the Department of National Defence contribute a large amount to vocational training?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: They do with regard to their own personnel, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I had hoped the acting minister would have been able to indicate that the federal government takes a great deal of pleasure in having participated in this program. We had a very long discussion about the defence production plans for the future. The minister pointed out that for the sake of the personnel involved it was necessary to have some indication that it was to be a continuing department. The

Supply-Labour
same thing applies to this department. The provinces have people who are involved who want to know whether the federal funds are to be cut oil or not. Unfortunately, there has been a feeling across Canada that the federal government is thinking of withdrawing from this very important field.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: My hon. friend is not helping. He is interested in seeing this continued. I do not know why he says we are withdrawing. What I have said is clear. We have an agreement now with the provinces running for a year in some cases. With regard to the apprenticeship agreements, we still have some running for ten years. We are going to have a dominion-provincial conference in which this, health matters and financial matters are all going to be discussed. My hon. friend would not expect me, or any other person having to attend a conference like that, to prejudge. We have to look at the whole problem. The government is very interested in this program. It has been a great program. We want to work out satisfactory schemes with the provinces, but I am sure that if we all approach this conference in the spirit of the over-all responsibility we shall achieve great success.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I merely want to say that as a member from a rural riding I should like to emphasize what is not generally realized, namely, that this legislation does something for rural education that has not been done before. I live in a small community where we have a competent school with 300 students, who have received very valuable benefits. It is true that the provincial government and the local people have supplied most of the money; but in Saskatchewan, as in many places, there are people who like to get assistance from the federal government. Had the federal government not come forward with proposals that such and such be done I am quite sure we would not have that modern school with 300 students. It would be a great pity now if the federal government pulled the props away.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: The hon. member is not helping the case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext: I merely want to emphasize the fact that the acting minister should take notice of the comments made by hon. members from all parts of this house asking that this work continue.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I will.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the acting minister has informed the committee that the matter of federal government participation in vocational training in Canada will be a subject to be discussed at the meeting in October between the federal government and the ten provincial governments. I have heard on numerous occasions that there is an inclination or feeling on the part of certain members of the cabinet that the federal government should vacate the field of federal aid for education because this is proving to be an embarrassment to the government. I do not know who those cabinet ministers are. I do not think vocational training enters the field of education and therefore I should like to feel that the cabinet is not considering vocational education as part of the problem which has to be met in regard to federal aid for education.
To the best of my knowledge all the provinces are now participating in and receiving help under this program, although there may be some of the smaller provinces which are not. I do know definitely that the province which feels most keenly about federal aid to education, the province of Quebec, is receiving aid under the vocational training program. I feel that the minister's answer is far from satisfactory to those who are charged with the responsibility of planning educational facilities in the dominion. As I understand it, the October conference is supposed to find ways and means of continuing after the expiration of the federal-provincial tax rental agreements. I understand that these agreements will not run out until 1957, and during what I think are our most crucial years in this particular field it would appear that those charged with responsibility at the local and provincial level of planning for technical education are left without any guidance.
Unless I heard him wrongly, the acting minister said that they will maintain interest. When you are a member of a local school board and faced with the problem of whether or not to spend millions of dollars on a building for a technical training school an assurance from the Acting Minister of Labour that the federal government will maintain interest is hardly good enough. I appealed to the minister before and I do so once again in the interests of vocational training in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I did not press this point before the lunch hour but, as we are still on it, the minister might go into a little more detail. We all enjoy listening to his musical voice when he is discussing his own department. I am sure that with this provocation he would outline in some detail the importance of the particular item. In view of the fact that ten years has passed since these arrangements were made, we should now look back and have some report as to whether they have been a worth-while investment.
Every member who has spoken has indicated that he thinks the work under this item should be continued and extended. I need not remind the house that all costs have increased very drastically since the arrangements were made in 1945, but I do not think that the federal government has proceeded to carry a fair share of the legitimate costs in connection with this item. The government should not have waited till now to indicate whether or not there is to be another ten-year period during which the provinces may count on extending their work.
If you take, for example, the courses under this vote for correspondence training, it is obvious that a tremendous burden would be placed on the provinces if they were to become responsible for working on correspondence courses for agriculture, including fruitgrowing and all the various other branches, in the building trade, with carpentry, electrical wiring, elementary joinery and so on. A great variety of commercial courses are offered. It is obvious that a tremendous amount of work and expense is involved in working out these programs. Certainly one set of courses is adequate for all of Canada. If the ten provinces now have to begin working at these courses and offering them to young people, it would place an unnecessary burden on the provinces. The hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out some of the problems that exist in these areas. I come from an agricultural area where unfortunately a great many of the young people cannot look forward to taking over the family farm.
