speechtext:
There are two matters I desire to raise under item 191, which concerns the administration of the unemployment insurance commission. I know that at this session there was a bill presented to consolidate and amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, but the two points I desire to raise do not deal with the act itself but rather with administrative policy under the act. Quite bluntly, Mr. Chairman, I am rather amazed to know that under the administration of an act of this nature the government or the unemployment insurance commission should enforce what amounts to despicable policies. One, I think, is definitely wrong, and the other is an absolute disgrace to our country.
The first point I should like to draw to the attention of the acting minister is the rulings being made as to where you live, and if you do not accept the job offered by the employment service, which is tied hand in hand with the unemployment insurance commission, then your benefits from unemployment insurance are wiped out. I am speaking on a matter of principle. It is not my desire to raise particular cases, it is the principle about which I am talking; but I am going to refer to the principle by giving an example.
I live in the city of Vancouver and have lived there now for 45 years. I know all the surrounding area. My own parents have had a home in White Rock, which is approximately 36 miles from the city of Vancouver. Here, we have a case of a woman who worked in the city of New Westminster on a parttime basis, but a part-time basis which enables her to come under unemployment

Supply-Labour
insurance regulations. For reasons which 1 do not need to go into now in any detail, she moved to White Rock. Before she leaves, she makes application for her unemployment insurance payments and gets it for one week. She moves to White Rock and wants her unemployment insurance. She also wants employment on a part-time basis. She is told there is employment in Cloverdale. Now, Cloverdale is between nine and eleven miles from White Rock. The employment is fulltime employment. She has to be on the job at nine and leave at five.
There is no transportation from White Rock to Cloverdale which would get a person to Cloverdale in time to go to work. The transportation there is not between White Rock and Cloverdale but between White Rock and Vancouver on the Pacific stage line; that is all there is. Since she cannot possibly get from White Rock to Cloverdale and back again unless she spends two hours early in the morning and two hours late at night-[DOT] she has children, by the way-she turned it down. What happened? Immediately she is notified by the unemployment insurance commission that she has lost her right to unemployment insurance because she turned down the job. I would not blame the minister for not knowing this, but the population of White Rock is 20 per cent higher than the population of Cloverdale. First of all, there is no transportation during business hours. I know it so well. I have lived there for 40 years in the summertime and I went to school there. I am giving this as one example of a principle. The unemployment insurance commission, for some reason or other, in some cases discriminates against a certain section of the country and indirectly tries to tell a person where they have got to live.
Now, sir, I say that is radically wrong. I want to tell the acting minister that I have made a very careful study of the example I have given, and I have taken it up through correspondence with the office here. They have given me the finest co-operation in investigating the situation. I say, sir, the principle is wrong in this case, and even although there is an appeal about it they do not know what they are talking about. If the acting minister cannot do it himself, I want him to have this entire situation investigated. I am convinced from the number of cases I have had that too often the unemployment insurance commission, tied in with the employment section of our federal government, is trying to direct, to an extent to which they have no right, where a person should live. If they do not coincide with the views of those who come under their jurisdiction, then those people are

completely discriminated against because they are eliminated from unemployment insurance benefits. I hate to say that, but that is my opinion. I wished to draw that to the attention of the acting minister.
My second point is one upon which I hope the acting minister will give an answer here now, even if he does not know the case itself. The principle concerns a great many of our citizens in Canada. Under the act, certain responsibilities are placed upon the government, the employers and the employees to make their contributions under the unemployment insurance provisions. I know of a Canadian citizen, Canadian born, who married in England. He brought his wife to Canada, and I do not blame him for that at all. I admire him for it. As happens in too many cases, there are troubles between the husband and the wife, which end in divorce. The wife goes back to England taking with her their daughter born of legal marriage. In England an order of the court is made. The father in Canada has to contribute toward the support of the child. I am glad to say that he accepted that responsibility in an honourable fashion. During all the years he worked he always paid the money for the support of his daughter, who has now reached the age of nine years.
Unfortunately however this man became unemployed a few months ago, and made application for unemployment insurance. I might add in passing that I have all the records. The unemployment insurance commission, established by parliament and administered by the government, told him he was a single man with no dependents. A single man receiving unemployment insurance would have a tough enough time to get by on the amount of money he receives, but most certainly a man who has a court order against him stating that he must support his child cannot pay anything on that order.
Yet I have the records to show that, so far as the unemployment insurance commission is concerned, this man is treated as a single man. Therefore he finds himself in the position where either he must starve to death, in which circumstance he could not contribute anything, or he must stand in contempt of court because of his failure to contribute to the support of a daughter born in legal wedlock.
As I said, I have the record of this case, and it reveals some astounding facts. His former wife took the child back to England. Recently the child has been in the United States with an aunt. This man can prove his legal divorce; at my request he is prepared to place the court order in my hands;

but he has already sent me a certain document indicating that, if his daughter were in the United States, the unemployment insurance commission could consider her as a dependent, and pay the money to him as a married man. However, because she was in England they cannot do so. Let me repeat that if the daughter were in the United States she could be considered a dependent, under the divorce order of the court, but if in England she could not be brought under the terms of the unemployment insurance provisions.
I do not care where the daughter or the wife is, the fact is that there is a court order which I can produce quickly if required, which states that he shall support his daughter. This he is prepared and always has been prepared to do. But now when he is unemployed this Liberal government administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act says, "When you are unemployed you are a single man." So he is left in a position where he is in contempt of court.
Sir, I think that is one of the most vicious, despicable things I have heard for a long time. I ask the acting minister to look into this case of the father against whom there is a court order to pay so much for his child. He can prove that he always paid it while he was employed, and has all the receipts to show it. I would ask that the minister take steps to see that the unemployment insurance commission accept him, not as a single man but as a man with a dependent, so that he may be given the status which would permit him to take care of his child, and not be held in contempt of court.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to add to what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver East. My subject, too, is man's inhumanity to man. I refer to something which may be regarded by many as a minor item, namely the provision of public washrooms in the offices of the unemployment insurance commission throughout Canada.
I wrote to the minister and received a reply dated July 19 from the acting minister. I thank him for sending me this well-written reply. I think I can advance my argument best by using parts of his letter. Among other things he said:
As you are perhaps aware, it is not the policy of the government to provide public toilets in government offices.
It may be that conditions in Ontario are different from what they are in British Columbia. I do know that in that province every little two-bit filling station wishing to 50433-425i
Supply-Labour
cater to the public offers the facilities of public washrooms. While some of them may be locked, one can always obtain the key and gain admission. I know they are widely used by those who patronize the filling stations, as well as by others.
Then the restaurants in British Columbia are required by law of the province and by civic health authorities to provide washroom facilities. I regret to learn that the law in Ontario is not insistent in this respect-or, if it is, the provision is not being enforced very severely. However, when this big enterprise, the government of Canada, operates a huge establishment such as the Alvin building in the city of Vancouver, it seems that it cannot offer public washroom facilities:
The minister goes on in his letter to say:
Because of the heavy traffic in unemployment insurance commission offices, however, it was decided some time ago to provide washrooms for public use on an experimental basis in some offices. Unfortunately the rooms were frequented by loafers and other undesirable persons and the public in general hesitated to use them.
In view of this experience public washrooms, if provided, would have to be supervised by attendants, and the cost of providing, cleaning, supervising and maintaining them would therefore be considerable.
For this reason the treasury board would be unlikely to agree to provide them. In view of these circumstances I regret that it will not be possible to provide public toilets in the Alvin building.
I find this most regrettable. I agree it will cost some money to provide the public with clean and adequate washroom facilities. However, as I mentioned at the beginning, this is a little sample of man's inhumanity to man. Here are the unemployed in the wintertime lined up for half an hour and more. They need washroom facilities. They have to desert their places in the line-up and walk possibly one or several blocks to use a washroom. They come back and they have to take a new place in the line-up. Therefore, instead of spending only half a day waiting for their meagre handout, they may have to spend a whole day. Also, new applicants for placement are often subjected to long interviews in order to ascertain adequately their abilities and to see what line of employment they might best be fitted into. I think it is a disgrace. We require little corner filling stations and little restaurants to provide the public with accommodation. You can walk into any office building or the office of any firm with whom you have dealings and all you need to do is to ask for a key and they will quickly supply you with a key to the washroom on the floor. The federal government of Canada, with a huge undertaking such as the unemployment insurance commission has in the city of Vancouver,

Supply-Labour
says: "We cannot afford to give the general public adequate washroom facilities." I think this is a disgrace.

The question I should like to raise has to do, not so much with registration or the administration of the act so far as the commission is concerned, but a matter of co-operation between the unemployment insurance commission and the provincial government. I know it is not a matter about which this government can order anything done, but perhaps by discussion something can be done to alleviate the situation. Some time ago-I think it was in June of last year -in the province of Manitoba at least an arrangement was made between the government at Vancouver and the federal government under which employees of the provincial government, particularly the public works department, could be brought under the act, but it was left optional to the employees whether they should come under the act.
Supply-Labour
The difficulty that has come about is perhaps a mechanical one, but it is rather an important one. There are a large number of employees of the provincial government who were not informed as to that situation. Some of them, of course, found out from their foremen or whoever was in charge of the job and proceeded to obtain their books and have their stamps put in and so on. Others who did not do so, when they were laid off later in the fall, discovered that they were not eligible because they had not presented their books. A few of these cases have been referred to me and I found that they were in perfectly good faith. These men simply did not know that such a provision had been made for them.
The reason I bring it up now is that perhaps there could be discussions between the commission and the provincial governments concerned, and I speak specifically of my own province, which is the only one that I know of where the difficulty has arisen. Perhaps some suggestions can be made that all employees who have the option of coming under unemployment insurance be notified officially by the commissioner of the province, perhaps by attaching a note to the pay cheques. In that way every employee would know he had the privilege or the option of coming under the act.
That would avoid a great deal of correspondence and difficulty several months later when, on the one hand, these employees claimed they were not notified and, on the other hand, the employees of the provincial government claimed they were notified by word of mouth or by rumour. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I should put a statement on the record at this time. The problems of the coal industry have been very much in the public eye recently and I think a statement of the situation as the government and the coal board see it would be helpful.
While there has been and continues to be a substantial increase in our requirements of this energy, this increase has been largely restricted to higher forms of energy such as electricity and liquid fuels. The main difficulty in the coal situation is that coal is losing some of its traditional markets to these more convenient fuels. In western Canada there are two different types of coal

and therefore of production and of marketing. The mines producing bituminous coal operate on Vancouver island and in the mountain areas of British Columbia and Alberta. The coal produced has been used almost entirely for steam raising purposes and the manufacture of coke. Most of these mines were opened to supply the railways, and some 70 per cent of the output has been sold for locomotive use.
In Alberta the coal costs about $6.30 per ton to produce, of which the labour cost amounts to about $3.45 per ton. The rate of production has been about 4 tons per man-day. This section of the industry has been badly hit by the conversion of steam locomotives from coal to oil and by the development of the diesel locomotive. Several mines have been closed. The railways claim that the change-over of fuel is a matter of economy and that to continue the use of coal would force them into a loss position and would lead to higher rates on all freight. This claim cannot be successfully challenged.
There is a market for industrial coal in Quebec and Ontario that consumed some 13 million tons in 1954. This coal is generally burned in large steam plants designed for the use of specific types of coal and operating at full capacity. There seems to be an idea that coal is about the same wherever it is found and can be used without difficulty in any type of plant. This is a basic fallacy and the facts should be more clearly understood.
A plant designed, for example, to operate economically on Nova Scotia coal with 33 per cent volatile matter and an ash that fuses at
2,000	degrees will not operate efficiently on western bituminous coal with 20 per cent volatile matter and an ash fusing point of 2,800 degrees. It is possible that it will operate in some fashion but not at a full efficient level.
The furnace equipment in Ontario and Quebec plants is generally designed for the type of coal that is most readily available. In Quebec, Nova Scotia coal or similar coal is usually supplied, while in Ontario most of the equipment requires a coal similar in characteristics to that produced in Pennsylvania and West Virginia. In the discussion of the estimates of the dominion coal board in 1952, I advised the house that a survey of the industrial coal users showed that approximately 1 million more tons of Canadian coal could be used by industry in Ontario. In that statement it was not made clear that of the additional capacity of 1 million tons, only some 275,000 tons was suitable for western coals, and much of this could only be on a part-time basis.
6737
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I would say here that the Ontario industrial consumer is generally a patriotic Canadian and anxious to use our native coal if it can be done without restricting the output of his plant or costing too much. There are firms in Ontario who can use, and are using, western coal at extra cost to themselves as a patriotic duty, and I feel that their co-operation should be mentioned here and appreciated. It is clear, however, that the Ontario industrial market for coal does not offer much relief to the hard-pressed western bituminous operator.
To secure what relief is possible, the government this spring increased the amount of subvention payable on western industrial coal moving to Ontario to $4 per ton and has also provided assistance on industrial coal moving to Manitoba. By this assistance, a market for some 200,000 tons has already been secured. The provision of more subvention on such a movement would not increase the tonnage to any great extent at this time, for the reason that the use of this type of coal is limited by the performance required in existing furnaces.
Industry in western Canada requires a considerable amount of fuel and a large part of the market is still supplied with coal. Oil and gas have offered stiff competition, and as more of these fuels are brought into full production, there may be further gains at the expense of coal. Even in the coal market, differences in the cost of production and of transportation have led to a decrease in the supply by bituminous mines, and a concurrent increase in the supply of cheaper locally mined subbituminous and lignite coals produced by strip-mining. This picture is not bright, Mr. Chairman, but nothing can be gained by refusing to face facts. The dominion coal board and the technical officials of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys have these problems under continuous study, but it would be unrealistic to say that there is any solution in sight whereby, under existing circumstances, these bituminous mines could be brought back into full production. There will remain some market for this coal, particularly the better quality, but any large-scale development will have to await the greater industrialization of the west or the depletion or diversion to other uses of the gas and oil that is presently in surplus supply.
The other type of western coal, sometimes known as domestic, has in the past supplied the household markets. Drumheller, Edmonton, Lethbridge and Coalspur have been the major fields and have marketed large tonnages from Victoria as far east as northern
6738	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys Ontario. These coals are meeting severe competition. Oil, gas and propane have substantially reduced the outlets, while the lower cost coals produced by strip mining in other western fields have cut heavily into the remaining markets. It is difficult to see any improvement in local markets because of the availability of gas and these competing fuels.
The Ontario market has always looked attractive to these domestic producers, but as I have reported on previous occasions to this house the poor storage qualities, high freight rates and seasonal restrictions on supply have held back developments. To this must now be added the fact that the Ontario domestic market, which used some 6,500,000 tons of coal and coke in 1945, has fallen to 4 million tons in 1954 and is still falling, owing to oil competition. Suggestions have been made that assistance should be provided on the sale of coal in western Canada in competition with locally produced gas and oil. I am sure that hon. members will all agree that any policy of subsidizing one particular form of Canadian energy against another would be unsound.
We have, however, in the regulations issued this spring increased the assistance payable on these coals moving to Ontario by 50 cents a ton, and have been advised by the operators this measure will be of some assistance. I have intentionally given the gloomy side of the western picture, but there are other phases which are not so dark. Some of the major operators in the Crowsnest pass are endeavouring to diversify their operations. I know of at least two companies that are embarking on very intensive exploration programs for base metals in the area. Others are engaged in lumbering and in the oil business in order to stabilize their business and to provide more employment for the people of that area.
The coal industry in Saskatchewan has maintained and even increased production, and is looking forward to wider markets when the new power stations presently being developed come into operation. In Alberta contracts are being let for two new large power stations, one of which will use coal at once while the other will use gas at first but will revert to coal when a more remunerative market is found for the gas. Both of these plants, however, will use the cheap strip-mined coal available in the immediate neighbourhood. Neither of these developments will provide much employment for the trained underground miner. It would appear that we are facing a technological revolution in the coal industry, and the most that can be done is to soften the blow to the older type operations.
tMr. Prudham.l

In eastern Canada the picture, while not cheerful, is not yet so dark as the western picture. In New Brunswick, there is a comparatively small but flourishing industry that has maintained and even bettered its position by increasing the efficiency of its production. The Nova Scotia situation is somewhat different. The railways have in the past provided an outlet for a substantial part of the production. The gradual change-over to diesel propulsion has reduced the railway market and promised to eliminate it in the not too distant future. This has been difficult for the mines on the mainland, in the Joggins, Cumberland and Stellarton areas because the railway outlet is particularly important to them. The closing of some of the older mines in these areas due to increasing physical difficulties in mining has kept output in a fair relation to the demand, but the future is uncertain because of the prospect of decreasing markets.
I made an interjection the other night during the consideration of the estimates of my colleague the Minister of Transport in reply to a statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South regarding the railway market. I stated that the industry in Nova Scotia had, in recent years, not fully supplied the market available on the Canadian National Railways. This was a true statement, Mr. Chairman, although perhaps I should have elaborated on it a little more at that time. The fact is that the entire maritime area of the Canadian National Railways is supplied by Nova Scotia coal. There is a considerable market available for Nova Scotia coal on the Canadian National in Quebec and Ontario, but the railway requires a sized and well prepared coal. With the increase in mechanization and the mines becoming deeper, the production of slack coal by the major company in Nova Scotia has been decidedly on the increase in recent years. The result is that if the major company were to supply all the coal market available on the Canadian National, that is the sized coal, it would not be able to dispose of all the slack. It is for that reason the railway market has not been fully supplied.
The mines on the mainland are, as I have said, facing decreasing markets owing to the increased cost of production. This is partly due to the depth of the coal and troublesome mining conditions. Mainland coal gets a fair local market, but oil is becoming more and more competitive. A subvention is available on this coal and some of it does move to Quebec under assistance. It may be that this market could absorb some further amounts, and I am sure the producers are endeavouring to secure other outlets.

Cape Breton remains as the most important area, in view of the number of employees and the comparative isolation from other sources of employment.
This area has not had any serious marketing difficulties until fairly recently. The mines have been undergoing a change-over to mechanical production, and the teething pains of this conversion have lasted longer and have been more severe than was expected. The mechanization plan, as submitted to the dominion coal board in 1948, was designed to increase the over-all output to some extent, to double the efficiency of production, and therefore substantially to reduce the cost and reduce the total labour force. It was expected that as the output increased from the improved efficiency the lower cost would enable the coal to find wider markets. At the same time the working force would gradually decrease, with the increasing production per man-day, and by the natural wastage through retirement and old age they expected to keep the industry in a healthy condition.
This program has not been realized. Production per man-day is only now beginning to increase slightly, while cost of production has actually increased over the period-* although a change is now evident with a slight drop in these costs.
Production from Nova Scotia mines in
1953-	54 was 2-15 tons per man-day. In
1954-	55 it increased slightly to 2-25 tons per man-day. This has meant that the coal at present costs has not been able to find wider markets. In fact, it has only retained the present outlets through the provision of greater amounts in subvention. The labour force has not declined through natural causes, as was planned, but has been held at a high level in order to maintain output. In this period, while a wider market could have been established, oil competition has grown more and more serious and now threatens a large proportion of the industry.
Over the last year there has been some improvement in efficiency of output and this is continuing into the early months of this year. This improvement together with the relatively high labour force is tending to increase the over-all production of coal. Unfortunately the opportunity to establish a wider market through lower costs has largely disappeared and outlets that would have been available have been lost to oil. Under these circumstances, it may become necessary to reduce total output to the market demands. In any event it is essential to do everything possible to retain the present market through reducing costs. This can only be accomplished in the opinion of the operators by the 50433-426i
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys closing of at least one of the highest cost collieries. This mine was closed on June 30.
There has been a request for further assistance by government to find wider markets. Recently the government agreed to extend subvention assistance up to $2.50 a ton for a trial shipment of 100,000 tons to Great Britain and a trial shipment of 20,000 tons to Germany. I understand that the shipment to Great Britain is presently moving, but that the sale to Germany has not yet been completed. I wish to emphasize that that assistance was extended on a trial basis only in order to see if they could get a foothold in those markets.
At the present time, Nova Scotia coal is moving as far west as Ottawa and supplies almost all the market from here east for coal of this type and characteristics. There is some imported coal used in Quebec but a careful investigation by the dominion coal board has shown that almost all is of a type and kind that is required for special purposes that cannot be filled by the maritime product. The cost of subvention on most of this coal is about $4.75 per ton although the over-all subvention for 1954-55 was $2.96. To find markets further west would cost from $5.75 per ton up to $7 and $8 in subvention assistance. In the last fiscal year, the subvention on Nova Scotia coal has been $8,689,018. There has been a payment of $224,555 under the Canadian Coal Equality Act; and also if you wish to delve further, there has been $350,000 in freight assistance for coal under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. In total, this amounted to over $9 million, or about $1.59 per ton on the total production.
In the Alberta and British Columbia area the subvention paid on bituminous coal only was $1,864,413, and on the domestic type alone, it was $499,465, a total of $2,363,878. These payments amounted to $2.67 per ton of bituminous coal moved, or 85 cents per ton produced, and $3.35 per ton of domestic coal moved, or 21 cents per ton produced. On all Alberta coals, the average subvention per ton of coal moved was $2.79 and on the overall production it was 52 cents. The industry also has the protection of 50 cents per ton tariff on imported bituminous coal.
The royal commission on coal in their conclusions recommended that the subventions as then existing should be maintained in principle, but added that the amount of assistance should bear a reasonable relation to the cost of imported coal. Good grade American bituminous coal is available at about $3.75 per ton at the mines or $8.25 to $8.75 at lake and river ports. The subventions I have outlined, together with the
6740	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys other assistance and the protective duty which is practically 15 per cent ad valorem, would seem to conform to this recommendation in a generous fashion.
The future of this basic industry depends upon the early realization of improvement in efficiency and reduction in cost that will enable it to retain the present outlets and capture a fair share of the new requirements.
The story would not be complete unless it was also pointed out that this loss of coal markets has not been confined to Canadian coal. Imports of bituminous coal from the United States have fallen from 22,753,000 tons some five years ago to only 15,683,000 tons this last calendar year. It is evident that the same competition faces American coal as is playing havoc with our own production even although the cost differentials as against oil are much less.
The government is doing everything reasonably possible to help the industry over this difficult transition period. The amount of money you are being asked to vote is somewhat higher than last year. In addition government agencies have been instructed to purchase Canadian coal wherever the cost is up to 10 per cent more than imported coals.
I might add that even before this directive was issued, out of a total of some 1,040,000 tons of coal purchased by government agencies, some 730,000 tons was of Canadian origin. We have also endeavoured to maintain markets for coal by requiring every government agency proposing to change to or to instal oil to submit their plans to the dominion coal board for investigation of the relative costs and of other factors.
The future of Canadian coal lies more and more in development of industry and in the growing demand for electric power. Co-ordination of these demands and the development of larger units of production would help through the lowered costs and greater efficiency of the larger units. Recommendations to this effect have been made by a consultant retained by the dominion coal board, Dr. Christie, to study the maritime situation, that is, the maritime power situation, and these have been passed on to the provincial authorities for their consideration.
The coal-fired turbine offers some hope for the future, but it must not be forgotten that these technical advances cannot be forced beyond a certain pace, and this project is no exception. It should also be remembered that this new engine may be found to operate more cheaply on lower grades of coal and that its development and use would not increase the outlet for higher grades.


At the present time the machine is not operating pending changes in design. As a result of the initial test runs, it became evident that certain modifications and adjustments were needed for the heat exchanger. It was thought advisable to make these adjustments before the test runs were completed so that more accurate data could be obtained. When these modifications are completed, test runs will be made over a sufficient length of time to determine the efficiency and the fuel costs for the use of locomotive or stationary engine purposes.
The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is asking for $110,000 this year for this project, which will bring the total expenditure to approximately $600,000. I might add that the developers of the project say that at no time have they been hampered by the lack of money. Every assistance has been given to the project and we are convinced that it could not be pushed faster. It is hoped that when the tests are finally completed commercial interests will undertake the development of a prototype locomotive or power unit.
From time to time we read about possible new uses for coal. There is no doubt that coal contains the basic building blocks necessary for the manufacture of many synthetics, also many chemicals such as ammonia and materials for fertilizer and a host of other uses.
Throughout the world research and experiments are being carried on. The fuels division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is keeping in close touch with these developments, and we are doing a considerable amount of research on our own.
About 50 employees of the branch are devoting most of their time to coal problems. There is a small-scale experiment on the hydrogenation of coal, but most of our efforts are directed toward assisting the industry in their briquetting and preparation problems.
In addition to the work on the coal-fired turbine, which I have mentioned, we have several teams in Alberta, British Columbia and Nova Scotia working with the companies on problems of mining, with special attention to pressure problems related to mining at depth.
At the present time natural gas is in plentiful supply in Canada and it is a more convenient and a cheaper source of material for synthetics than possible coal derivatives.
In conclusion, I am convinced there will remain a sizeable market for Canadian coal. This may increase substantially over the next 10 or 20 years as our country expands.

In the immediate future, however, there will be very serious changes and transitions within the coal industry.
The greatest challenge facing the coal industry at the moment is that of reducing the cost of production in order to meet competition. You cannot separate the cost of production from the marketing problem. If the industry is successful in reducing costs, the markets will be correspondingly improved.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the outline given by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is not one to convey any substantial measure of encouragement to the people who are dependent upon coal mining as the source of their livelihood, nor to those who may regard the production of coal as an essential part of our general economy.
The minister has said that it would not be wise to give any unduly favourable impression as to the situation which would not be supported by the facts. I should think everyone will agree with that. Nevertheless, there must be a recognition of the fact that coal is one of the basic requirements of the economy of this and of other countries, and what is even more important is that it is a key industry in the province of Nova Scotia, where it employs some 10,000 to
11,000	miners.
The difficulties that are befalling the coal industry in Canada are not unknown elsewhere. They have been encountered in the United States where the coal industry has been so much a part of their great period of development. There has been, however, a different situation in the United States. In yesterday's New York Times I read an article under the heading "Recovery on the Way in Coal Industry." This very long, well-written article on the situation in the coal industry in the United States does not suggest for a moment that their troubles are over; but it does point out that there has been an improvement and that there has been a vigorous attempt to seek new markets as well as to employ coal in new ways.
They have achieved some substantial improvement there by doubling the export of coal, and of course they have seen an improvement related to the use of coal for the electric utilities and the steel mills which have been increasing so much in production within the past year. The fact does remain, however, that in the United States they are now apparently on the upgrade. The situation there is not one which presents some of the problems that we have here.
Undoubtedly, one of the major aspects of our problem is the fact that some 60 per cent of the whole consumption of coal in
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys Canada is within 200 miles of the cities of Montreal and Toronto, while the supplies of Canadian coal are a very long distance away from those centres.
It would seem that one of the things that must be borne in mind in any examination of this subject is that coal is likely to be in the future, as it has been in the past, a steady, continuing source of vital fuel supplies. There are more glamorous fuels; there are more dramatic types of fuels, such as gas and oil; but those can be readily exhausted within comparatively short times in terms of the history of nations. I am not suggesting for a moment that the time is short in the life of human beings. But in the long range of national history these could be diminishing resources. We are likely to look to coal in the years ahead as we have in the past.
One of the things which must be borne in mind in dealing with this coal problem is that in Nova Scotia, where it is more vital to the economy of that province than it is to Alberta, vital though it may be there, many of the mines are submarine mines. If as a result of continuing displacement of the use of that fuel those mines cease to be worked they might be lost forever. There is, moreover, a very serious problem that can arise if whole communities in Nova Scotia, dependent as they are upon the production of coal, find it necessary to seek work elsewhere and the skill and family traditions of association with that type of work are lost. It would be most difficult to restore our position in the production of coal at some time in the future.
There can be no question but that the difficulties are tremendous. This is something which is of concern not only to Nova Scotia, to the maritime provinces and to the western provinces as well where coal is mined; it is something that is essentially a part of the whole Canadian economy. The coal industry is at the crossroads, and unless something is done to revitalize it the impact upon the lives of many Canadians is going to have far-reaching consequences, and there could well be serious dislocations in some parts of our economy.
The minister has said that we must look to greater industrial expansion in the areas where coal is mined. That is one place where at a time like this the government can contribute to the solution of this problem. Almost one-half of the money being spent by the government goes directly or indirectly into some aspect of national defence or the preparation for defence. A great part of that money is allocated in the form of special undertakings under the direction of different
6742	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys departments of government but mainly under the Department of Defence Production. We have urged that the government facilitate the decentralization of industrial production through the influence it has through contracts of various kinds for defence and other production. The minister has stated that this is the course which they see as an immediate solution. If that is so surely there should be a greater effort on the part of the government to encourage industry in those areas where coal is now produced.
Another use of coal on which the minister has touched is for the production of electricity. The minister stated that the services of experts have been sought for the purpose of considering the possibilities in this type of development. He tells us that this information has been passed on to the provincial government for their consideration. No one has been a stronger advocate than I of the full exercise of their constitutional jurisdiction by the provincial governments, but certainly there are some cases where a development of this kind could be stimulated as part of the general development of those essential power requirements in connection with our defence and other production.
If it is a fact that the report made by the experts who inquired into this subject suggests the practical possibility of the production of electrical energy from coal, then it might well be that in co-operation with the provinces, just as the dominion government has co-operated recently in the production of electrical energy in New Brunswick, suggestions might be made as to the ways in which this could be done to the advantage of employment in those provinces and the general economy of Canada. I have suggested before in this house during the discussion of this subject that we might well consider the successful production of electrical energy in Germany and Russia from coal, particularly from low-grade deposits of coal where the gas is actually burned underground and power produced at most satisfactory cost levels.
Then again there is the possibility of a wider employment of coal for chemical and synthetic production. I do not intend to enlarge on that. Everyone knows that there has been a very wide employment of coal in the chemical field, and today many of the things we use in the form of ordinary consumer goods are the chemical by-products of coal.
There are possibilities of positive developments along this line. Undoubtedly the situation is serious and it is likely to become much more serious unless positive and vigorous


policies are adopted by the government. The subventions which have been paid by the government-and increased subventions are now being asked for-have not prevented a reduction in the use of coal as the result of increasing competition by other fuels. Since 1950 coal has played a substantially smaller part in supplying Canada's total energy requirements. Coal production has declined by 22 per cent, but this decline in production has not been evenly distributed. From 1950 to 1954 the Alberta output declined by 3,257,000 tons or 40 per cent; the British Columbia output declined by 24 per cent; the Nova Scotia output declined by 640,000 tons or 10 per cent, while coal production in New Brunswick and Saskatchewan actually expanded after world war II. The pattern is not uniform, and the problem is one that affects the whole Canadian economy.
It is fortunate in many ways that the reduction has been smaller on a percentage basis in Nova Scotia than in some other parts of Canada, in view of the dependence of that province upon coal production for its financial resources and for employment. However, the threat continues with the possibility of greatly increased use of gas and oil-particularly of gas-in the great industrial centres of central eastern Canada, and the threat will become more serious in the future. If western Canadian gas is supplied to the Toronto and Montreal areas, or if under any mutual arrangement other gases are supplied in those areas in exchange for western gas, the demand for coal would undoubtedly be diminished to some substantial extent.
Therefore this problem is one which calls for vigorous and positive action which will encourage the industry to maintain its position during the intervening period until the time when wider use may be made of coal. It is something in which all Canadians must feel a direct interest, even if they come from provinces which are not dependent on coal for employment or their local economy. The fact that the economy of the maritime provinces is lagging is largely related to this problem. Therefore we must all take an equal interest in finding a temporary solution that will maintain the coal industry and, above all, maintain the employment of Canadians engaged in that activity and trained for that work. We must also be looking to the future for the wider employment of that fuel in the years ahead.
There is one subject the minister did not mention. In this country we have resources unparalleled in their quantity in any other country with a similar population. Few nations with any population, large or small,

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
have comparable resources. It has been said before, and it should be said over and over again, that if we use our own resources in Canada for the employment of Canadians in this country, then we need not worry about the optimum of population, to use that ugly word. We can feed far in excess of 100 million people; we can clothe that number; we can keep them warm; we can provide all the things that are needed. Therefore one of the ways of meeting the problem with which we are confronted is a positive, selective and well-organized plan of immigration which will in itself promote the consumption of these fuels in the areas where they are produced.
Not only should immigration policy be directed to the selection of the right type of immigrant. It should also be directed to the encouragement of the settling of newcomers to Canada in areas where a decentralized industry could give them employment, and in that way make economic use of the resources we possess. Undoubtedly there should be a greater use of coal in the years ahead if we encourage a wider development of industry in those areas close to the coal itself, whether that be in the maritimes, in Alberta, in British Columbia or in any other part of Canada.
There is another threat with which we are confronted, and that is the deepening of the St. Lawrence river, which most of us hail as a great advantage to Canada. It is of tremendous advantage to the general economy of Canada, and undoubtedly of the greatest advantage to the part of Canada close to that development. Nevertheless the deepening of the St. Lawrence river and the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway is going to make coal from the United States even more competitive with Canadian coal than it is at the present time.
This merely serves to emphasize the need for balancing encouragement in other fields as well. The natural resources that are coming into production, such as iron and the other base metals which will be encouraged by the St. Lawrence seaway, should be fabricated as much as possible in this country. That fabrication should be encouraged by government policies which will make it advantageous to process those raw materials to the most advanced point practicable in Canada, for the employment of Canadians here in our own country.
These are, of course, general statements. It may very profitably be said that this is a practical subject which can be solved only by cold realities. That is true. It can be solved only by cold realities interpreted in dynamic policies. The realities are that people will employ the type of fuel they find
most suitable for their own requirements. The realities are that they will undoubtedly turn to some of the fuels that can be more readily transmitted to the furnaces of industry and to the homes of our people generally.
The minister himself has touched on certain demands that will increase employment in our mineral areas by increasing the consumption of coal. There are policies directed to the wider fabrication of our resources of other kinds which would increase that demand. Above all, there are policies of encouragement of this industry by methods that may be found satisfactory elsewhere. The minister has spoken of an experimental shipment of fuel overseas. People in other countries need fuel. Many nations are without it. Let us press for the wider marketing of that fuel overseas because, particularly in the case of Nova Scotia, it is at the seaboard.
Whatever the methods, let us approach this subject recognizing that it is not something of interest only to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Alberta, British Columbia or to any other area of Canada as a local problem. It is part of the problem of all Canadians, relating to the development of our resources and the employment of our own people. Whatever immediate solutions are found, I submit that the best long-term solution is to encourage the fabrication of our own resources, which will expand the need for fuel for industry and other purposes in this country, and to follow policies that will populate this country with suitable immigrants who can make homes here and thus help to create employment with the almost limitless resources we possess. The solution of this problem is part of the great challenge facing all Canadians to fabricate our resources in Canada and to expand the whole development of our country by intelligent and understandable policies of Canadian production for the advantage of Canadian citizens in our own country.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys with a great deal of interest, but I do not think he left very much encouragement with the house so far as the rehabilitation of the coal industry is concerned. However, I will say that it is only within the last few years that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has done anything in the matter of trying to get a better understanding of the coal industry on a national basis. I spent a good many years in the house talking about coal, but what I said just went on the record and that was the end of it. However, I will say that since the formation of the dominion coal board and since the minister took over
6744	HOUSE OF
Supply

Mines and Technical Surveys the department an attempt has at least been made to understand and do something about an industry that was in pretty bad shape when the department began to take a square look at it.
For a good many years this department was something like fisheries and the post office. If there was someone who had to be given a seat in the cabinet so as to satisfy the requirements of geographical representation he was generally pushed into this department so he would be out of the way. If some federal department had taken the interest years ago that is being shown today, when we are locking the door after the horse has been stolen, we might not be discussing the kind of thing we are talking about today.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the Leader of the Opposition and the generalizations he made with respect to our resources and the coal industry. Generally speaking we are all agreed on what the problem is, but I would point out to him that so far as decentralization of industry is concerned, practically every year for at least twelve years, until I got discouraged, I had a resolution on the order paper suggesting that the government should undertake decentralization of industry so as to make for a better balanced economy and to provide protection in the event of the kind of war we may anticipate in the future. But like other resolutions it was discussed, what was said went on the record, and it was forgotten. What the Leader of the Opposition has suggested may be a good long-range program, but at this stage of the game I do not think it is going to solve the immediate problem.
This business of the coal industry being in difficulties is not something new. I have taken a look at some of the reports made in connection with the industry over the years.
I took a look, for example, at the report of the royal commission set up in 1926 under Sir Andrew Rae Duncan. If you read that report you will see that it deals with exactly what we are talking about this afternoon, markets, costs, the stepping up of production and the difficulties of marketing our coal in competition with United States coal. In 1932 another royal commission under Sir Andrew Rae Duncan was established by the government of Nova Scotia. In his report he makes a pretty thorough survey of the industry. He points out exactly what was pointed out in 1926 and what we are saying today. He refers to the need for economies, reduction in costs, the stepping up of man-day production and the difficulties of meeting competition. At that time, of course, he recommended a reallocation of collieries and the concentration of production. That program [DOT] [Mr. Giffis.l

was carried out. That is why you have two or three mines operating on one shaft. But it did not solve the problem. Of course many of the recommendations made by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan were not carried out, particularly those having to do with welfare plans and so forth.
Then came the Carroll commission, the latest one, which produced a pretty comprehensive report in 1946. Of course it was a minority recommendation in that report that resulted in the setting up of the dominion coal board. The board has done a very good job in so far as its powers will permit it to do so. It is an efficient and effective organization at the national level, but I should like to remind the committee that regulation of the coal industry either in the east or the west is not the prerogative of the federal government. Coal as a resource is under the direct control of the provincial governments with respect to the operation of mines, the letting of leases and costs of production. These are matters that are outside the jurisdiction of the dominion coal board or the minister's department. These matters are under the control of the companies operating the mines and the provincial governments which lease the property to the companies. To some extent the miners' union must also take some responsibility so far as policing the whole operation in the interests of the men is concerned.
I make this statement because many times you see newspaper reports that are very misleading. With respect to matters that come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the province or the management of the company you will find the federal government being attacked because they are not doing this and this and this. I do not say that to defend them, but merely from the point of view of clarification in order to get the question in its proper perspective.
The Carroll commission report made a lot of recommendations, one of which was the setting up of a coal board. The coal board has at least provided a national body to do research and keep in touch with the industry east and west. In my judgment it has done a lot to implement the recommendations of the Carroll commission. There were some 14 very important recommendations. I have a return in my hand indicating which ones were implemented and which were not and the reasons why. It is a very comprehensive return, because it shows that practically all the major recommendations of the Carroll commission report were carried out. That is as far as the dominion coal board could go.
Another matter is dealt with in the Carroll commission report that I have mentioned to

the minister a good many times. I refer to the fact that a lot of United States coal is coming into the country and being used in markets that were held prior to 1939 and 1940 by Nova Scotia coal. In coming into the Ontario market that coal is receiving the regular subvention rates that prevail at the present time. The rates have changed a bit because freight rates have changed, but when freight rates changed the subvention rates were increased to offset any increase in freight rates.
At page 130 of the Carroll report the commissioner makes an observation that I have made a good many times in the house with reference to United States coal. He points out that while during the war it was necessary to drop the Ontario market as far as Nova Scotia coal was concerned because of the shift in our market to bunker coal, it was distinctly understood that when the war was over the Dominion Coal Company was going to import coal from the United States to supply the Ontario market simply for the purpose of holding their customers in the aftermath of the war. The commission had this to say:
During recent years the company has sold a considerable quantity of coal purchased by them from the United States. The tonnage reached a high figure of 1,964,136 short tons in the year 1944, which approximates the tonnage of Dominion coal sold in the same market prior to the war. It would appear that this condition was due to a declining production in the Nova Scotia mines and also an increased demand for Scotia coal from the steel industry. The net profit realized by the company on United States coal for 1944-
And so forth. The loss of that market was not due to any decline in production in the Nova Scotia mines. The commission is in error there. I think what has happened has been that instead of carrying out the original intention of handing back that 2 million ton market in Ontario to Nova Scotia, the same company that is operating the coal mines in Nova Scotia has been importing this coal. I want the minister to clear this up before we finish his estimates this time. I also want him to explain to this house who is the Dominion Import Company, located in Montreal. Is it a subsidiary of Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, and how much United States coal has it imported into this country from 1954 up to date?
The Carroll report is very definite that they imported approximately 2 million tons of United States coal in 1944, and according to this report they marketed it in a market which belonged to Nova Scotia previous to 1939. There is no use trying to fool ourselves. There is no use trying to protect somebody who is not doing what is right. I am not prepared to either kick around the minister
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys of mines or the provincial government of Nova Scotia if the people who are mining and marketing that coal in this country are not playing ball with the Canadian people or the Canadian government. It is not doing anyone any good to try to screen people who are trying to pull that kind of sideline stunt with respect to that industry.
Now, that is not my statement; it is the statement of the royal commission headed by Hon. Mr. Justice W. F. Carroll, whose report was tabled in this house in 1946. I want the minister to clean up that particular angle. If there is a market there for 2 million tons, a market which previous to the war belonged to that company, then the minister wants to clear that up, because that market certainly should have gone back to Nova Scotia coal. If it had, we would not have the problem we have today in that particular industry.
Another thing I should like to point out is that during the time the Carroll commission sat there appeared before that commission representatives of the coal operators in the United States. They presented a brief to the commission on behalf of the Consolidated Coal Company; the Hanna Coal and Ore Company; North American Coal Corporation; Pittsburgh Coal Company; Rochester and Pittsburgh company, and the Valley Camp Coal Company. If you read this brief you will find that the coal policy of the United States is very much tied up with the valuable market they have in Canada. It is a pretty powerful influence when you are dealing now with a coal policy in Canada in connection with a declining industry. I can understand the decline of the industry in British Columbia, where something replaced coal in the economy of the province. They have a steel industry, and they have their forest products. In Alberta there is the oil development and natural gas. In those provinces the industry became a casualty through our own products.
But this is not true in Nova Scotia. Our main competitor in Nova Scotia is United States coal. It is outside fuel that has been imported into this country. While natural gas has had some effect and oil has had some effect in the dieselization of the railroads, nevertheless the main competitor for Nova Scotia coal today is coal that is coming from the United States. Do not forget, as this brief presented to the Carroll coal commission points out, the coal that comes into Canada from the United States is coming from the largest mine with the highest production, the most highly mechanized mine with the lowest cost.
In western Canada the industry became a casualty to our own natural products, but in Nova Scotia the reverse is true. We are
6746	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys becoming a casualty at this time, and we have been under difficulty for a great many years, because there has been an unrealistic policy on the part of the government concerning the importation of United States coal. I just want to leave that with the minister, because you have to take a look at the United States position. They are putting approximately 24 million tons of coal into this country every year, and they are doing it in a planned way from the cheapest areas and with freight assistance from the United States government.
As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, the St. Lawrence seaway is going to create further difficulties for the Nova Scotia coal industry. I said that in the house. In fact I was the only man in the house who opposed the St. Lawrence seaway for that particular reason. Do not forget that right now water-borne coal from the United States is getting up into the Ontario markets along the lakes. Large import companies in Montreal and throughout Ontario, with quite a capital investment, are storing huge amounts of United States coal. This is all water-borne at the present time, and at a very low rate.
Of course some of these companies have their own on-company service rate, which is pretty low. It is five mills per ton mile; that is the rate from Rouses Point down to Moncton. Our own service rate from Sydney up to Moncton runs up to 11 mills per ton mile. The United States is given a freight rate break in this country, unless it has been changed very recently. I know that two years ago I tried very hard to find out why United States coal was shipped from Rouses Point down as far as Moncton at five mills per ton mile while our own coal from Sydney to Moncton was costing about 11 mills per ton mile.

This agreement the railways had with the government, I do not know how many years ago-

The on-service rate. I understand it was abrogated by the C.N.R., without consultation with the government. An effort was going to be made to straighten it out. However, I point this out only to show that in this matter of competition the Canadian industry, so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, can never be competitive with coal from the United States. The thing we have to determine, so far as our industry is concerned, is whether or not it is essential to the community. If it is essential to the community then it has to be supported and maintained. If it is not essential to the community then it should be scrapped. But I am reasonably sure that the Nova Scotia industry is essential to the community.
Anyone who talks about meeting competition, so far as Nova Scotia coal is concerned, with coal from the United States, is not being realistic, because that can never be brought about. You will never cut costs in that industry to a point where you can meet competition from the United States. I am sure the chairman of the coal board, who has taken a long look at the problem, will agree with that statement. The mines in Nova Scotia are deep, submarine mines. They are getting old. There is a very long haul, high pumping costs, high pressures they have never even thought about in the United States. In other words the Nova Scotia industry is a high-cost industry, and it cannot be compared with the industry in the United States, because they do not have those costs over there. They do not have the high pressure; they do not have the gaseous conditions we have; they do not have our difficulties in ventilation, our long hauls, our high pumping costs, our power costs, because our mines are submarine and their mines are not submarine.
There is no comparison between the two industries, and there never will be any comparison so far as production costs are concerned. To continue to talk about competition in the laid-down costs of this commodity, competition with the United States commodity, as it might be used by the Canadian National Railways in either the central or

the eastern region, is unrealistic. It cannot be done. I do not blame the C.N.R. for talking along those lines. They are running a railroad, and it is their job to make money. If they do not, they have to come before a committee of this house and tell why. But it is up to the dominion coal board and the minister to realize that the problem is not one of competition. The problem is whether that industry is worth maintaining; whether we need it, and I am sure you will say that we do need it.
Second, I think the attitude of the company is wrong in setting a production target of 7,500,000 tons a year. That is an unrealistic target and cannot be attained, certainly not in the industry they have today. If they were sensible and fixed a production target' of 5 million tons a year; if they planned for that production and improved their methods, it might be done. But it should be understood that' they should not try to reach for the moon and sweat it out of the hides of the men, in an effort to attain a production target that is absolutely impossible in the kind of industry they have today. I think a 5 million ton industry is a reasonable one down there, and I think there is a market for that amount of coal from that province for a good many years to come; and it would not be hard to get. The people who operate should put their cards on the table and be frank with those who want to help them rather than make a lot of wild statements such as we see from time to time. They are just putting up a smoke screen.
Then as to the development of power in the maritime provinces, it must be said that the federal government did try to do something along those lines. At least it sent in a thermo-power expert in the person of H. E. Christie, and he reported back in August of 1954. I imagine his report was made to the government. A second report was made to the dominion coal board on September 20. I shall not take time to read them, but they point out very definitely that in the development of thermo-power in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, someone must be prepared to give up sovereignty. It is pointed out that the development of small units all over the place is not economical.
He does not give any new data. What he says, we have known for a good many years; but now that we have it from an expert we believe it. He believes if they would concentrate at some point in the three provinces and develop a large power project from coal, there is a possibility of meeting the power demands of the three maritime provinces by some centrally placed industry, managed,

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys handled and supported by the three provincial governments. Which two of the three will give up their sovereignty, I do not know. It will be something like the United Nations, everyone wants to do everything, but no one wants to give up a little power. But this is a matter which should be followed up. The coal board should follow it up and develop thermo-power in the maritime provinces. That would be a partial solution.
Personally I do not think we have hit our real competition yet. While we are struggling with the competition we have today, the time is not far distant when Alberta natural gas will be coming clean through to Quebec city. If that ever happened-and certainly it is something we should think about, so far as the coal industry is concerned-it would be serious. I know they would have financial difficulties, difficulties which may never be met. It would be a doubtful proposition to tie the great industries of Quebec to a natural gas supply that has to be brought
3,000	miles across the country by pipe line. A lot of things can happen to a pipe line. Unless you have a stand-by, to link yourself up to natural gas from Alberta to maintain the industrial set-up in Quebec and Ontario in my judgment would be a pretty doubtful proposition.
I think that was clearly demonstrated during the war, when southern Ontario depended upon American natural gas. When the Americans wanted it for themselves they shut off our supply, and there was a great scramble all through this part of the country when people were trying to convert their heating units from gas back to coal and oil. There was quite an upset, and I do not think many people will forget it.
However, we must plan for that. If natural gas is coming into that end of the country two or three years from now, then it is the responsibility of the federal government, the provincial governments and the operating coal companies to sit in and make plans now. They should not wait until the pipe line is down in this part of the world and then start hollering for relief. These things should be planned ahead.
I have spoken on this subject a good many times and I do not intend to take long today. I shall have some questions to ask the minister as we proceed with the items, because there are two or three things he should straighten out. When the minister answered me a few nights ago, or when he picked up the discussion the Minister of Transport and I were having on the matter of the Canadian National Railways purchasing Nova Scotia coal, the minister came out flat-footed and
6748	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys said the company could never supply the available market of the C.N.R.-period. I am glad to know that he completed the statement this afternoon and said it was a matter of getting the right size of coal and a matter of being able to meet the competition, as Mr. Gordon said.
I should like to say this to the minister. The big difficulty today seems to be the high percentage of slack the Dominion Steel and Coal company is producing. That does not surprise me, because if one goes back into the records ten years ago, when we were discussing the heavy equipment to be used underground in those mines, he will find that I said at that time that one of the factors that would be wrapped up in that operation was that they would get 70 per cent slack production. You cannot send heavy equipment into a mine that far underground, with the pressures they have, and start to chew it up without pretty well pulverizing the coal.
I always felt that type of equipment was very unrealistic in coal mines such as we have in Nova Scotia. I know in all of my experience underground-and I worked underground a long time, not, mind you, as a guy who walked around and looked around, but as a miner who dug coal-it was impressed upon me that I should get the coal as big as possible. You were continuously probing for methods and explosives that would cut your coal and blast it in such a way as to get it as large as possible, because that is the kind of coal you can market. I had no difficulty in seeing that this heavy equipment would pulverize the coal underground, and I am not surprised. They may have to change their methods of mining.
1 could ask a lot of questions, Mr. Chairman. I know not much can be accomplished by making a speech on this business. There are one or two things the minister should keep in mind. First, this is not a new problem. Second, our main difficulty, as far as Nova Scotia is concerned, is competition with United States coal. Our potential difficulties may come from natural gas, but right now and in the past it has been United States coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: And oil.

And oil within the last couple of years. But what we have lost to oil would not make very much difference in marketing the coal we can mine in Nova Scotia if we could meet United States competition on the railroads. There is a huge market there. Millions of tons of coal were imported by the C.N.R. last year and used largely in the central market. I think a market can be

found for our coal under the present subvention arrangements, provided we get the right type of coal. That is the company's business. That is not my business nor the minister's business. We cannot make that coal for them. That is their business.
The minister, through his department, even if the coal board has to be expanded, should be recognizing and planning for the fact that not only coal is going to be in difficulties in a few years. We have developing in this country four or five different potential fuels. If we allow them to grow up in a hodgepodge way, one competing with the other, they will all be in difficulties and we will not have any fuel industry. I believe the time has come in this country when we should have a body like the coal board, but expanded.
I believe there should be a regulatory national body in this country. The personnel of that body should take a look at the hydroelectric industry, the natural gas industry and the coal industry and determine, after a survey of the country, where these different fuels could be applied to the best economic advantage. Let us not forget for a minute that just around the corner is atomic energy. We should ascertain whether, in the light of the possibilities of atomic energy, we are being smart in spending so much money in developing other fuels and other types of power that may become obsolete in a few more years, rather than sticking to the old, conventional thing until the real thing is ready.
That type of body is needed in this country. To enable that type of organization to function we need legislation that would lay down a national fuels policy; we need a body that would be able to sit down with the government from time to time to map out, to plan and to bring some sanity into our whole fuel industry of the future.
The upset in coal, in textiles and in other industries comes about because nobody has taken a square, national look at the industry; that is, national in all its aspects. Fuel and power are basic to the whole economy of the country. They are in trouble. Many people will say this is nationalization. Anyone who takes that position is just talking sheer nonsense. I am not suggesting that you should take over anything. I am merely suggesting that you have a planning and regulatory body composed of competent people, who could guide the fuel and power requirements of this country so the maximum good will accrue to the country.
That is not nationalization, socialization, or anything else. It is exactly the kind of thing you had to do in the air with Trans-Canada Air Lines. What kind of picture

would you visualize in this country today if there was not some regulation in the air? It would be crazy. Take the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Not many people in the country would tune in very often unless there was some regulation of the air waves. Nobody is interfering with anybody's freedom. I merely suggest that we have a fuels industry, which I think is much more important than any other industry in this country, because without fuel and power the country would stagnate. To raise the hue and cry of nationalization when I suggest a national fuels policy along these lines is to be unrealistic. You have the machinery now. You would merely have to add to it people who are familiar with atomic energy and other types of fuel.

After the minister finished speaking this afternoon one of the members sent over a note to me, in which he said, "This sounds to me like a funeral oration on the coal industry." I do not think that. I think greater interest is being shown in it today than ever before in this country. Many people are taking an interest in it. The fact that the Leader of the Opposition recognized the importance of the matter this afternoon was also of some considerable encouragement, because most members know that in the past I have made many speeches on this subject and have moved many resolutions, but I received very little vocal support on it.
I say that this industry, rather than dying today, is on the way back. I believe it is going to come back and make a contribution in the future that is not visualized today. I do not think we can depend upon oil and gas to the extent we are apparently doing at this time. I can see this country expanding; and if we ever have 100 million people,
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys as is visualized by the Leader of the Opposition, we are going to need a lot of fuel. There is no sure way of knowing how long our oil or gas will last, but you can measure with some degree of accuracy your solid fuels.
I have taken longer than I intended, but I shall have a few more remarks to make at the appropriate time.
