speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after three hon. members get finished telling something that is not very hard to tell, there is but little left for the fourth speaker. I represent one of the really great coal-mining constituencies in Canada, and naturally I feel most unhappy about what is taking place in respect of coal.
I appreciate the force and validity of all the minister has said as regards the industry, and I realize that right now things look pretty dark. But I do believe that something can be done, I think it is important that we keep our coal industry in such working condition that at least in case of emergency it might be able to supply a serious need. I believe there are possibilities of devising ways and means whereby coal can be processed into a wide variety of substances which are now being produced from other raw materials which perhaps we cannot spare as easily as we can spare coal.
I believe I have said about all there is left to say in a constructive way. It is hard for anyone in the Lethbridge constituency to be convinced that when 15 million tons of coal are brought in from the United States every year, it is not possible to obtain just a little more of that market for Alberta. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South has referred to Nova Scotia I think I would be most presumptuous if I tried to talk for that province after the hon. member has finished. I shall leave Nova Scotia's case in his hands.
Ever since I came here, almost 20 years ago, I have believed that the story given to me in explanation of why so much coal was brought in from the United States just was not quite as sound as it seemed. I have always felt that there was a lot of window dressing, or perhaps camouflage would be a better word. I think things have been done in respect of the coal industry of western Canada which did not need to be done. I have always felt that we should have had a larger share of this market. I am sure it would have been better for Canada if we had. It must be remembered that we have this year an adverse trade balance of something like $650 million with the United States, speaking from memory. Last year we had an adverse trade balance with that nation of something over $350 million. When we realize just how serious that is for Canada

In saying that I do not criticize the minister, as I realize that practically all I have talked about happened before he came on the scene. Mr. Chairman, the closure of No. 1-B colliery at Glace Bay at the end of June brings into sharp focus the urgency of the problems that now face the Nova Scotia coal industry and, indeed, illustrates very clearly the public anxiety that is attached to any reduction in the working force of coal miners of Nova Scotia. The principal reason for closing this colliery was the diminishing market, which in this current year experienced a decline of half a million tons. Of course I join with the minister in expressing the view
6752	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys that you cannot speak realistically about markets unless at the same time you consider production costs, because these latter obviously determine the rate at which the producer can put his product on the market.
The case of No. 1-B colliery is worthy of some analysis, because it represents a point of departure or a point of crisis in the coal industry in Nova Scotia. For that reason I want to spend a few moments talking about the recent experience of this colliery. The costs of production for this colliery for the year 1953 were substantially higher than the average cost of producing coal in the other Cape Breton coal mines. But at the same time, if the costs of production of this colliery had been brought down to a level comparable with the costs in all the other coal mines in Cape Breton, we would still have the problem of disposing of half a million tons of coal. To put the problem another way, No. 1-B was for the past year the high cost colliery, but if its costs had been at the same level as other collieries the present problem would still be in existence, and the problem of disposing of half a million tons of coal would still be present.
At the conference held in Halifax this spring, which was attended by representatives of the provincial and federal governments, the management and the united mine workers, no one disputed the assertion that it was impossible to dispose of this amount of coal in the domestic market at the current subvention rate and at the price at which the producer could put his coal on the market. Therefore the decision to select No. 1-B for closure was simply because it happened to be for the past year the high cost producer. Because in the present situation an immediate general reduction in cost was not forthcoming, and because when there was no disposition to increase the subvention rate beyond its present level, there was a sudden realization of the need to turn away from the domestic market and to seek markets in the United Kingdom.
I think at this point the house should be made aware of the excellent co-operative arrangements that existed among the provincial government, the dominion coal board and the management in developing a new market for coal in the United Kingdom. I believe the initial overtures were made to the fuel board in the United Kingdom by Premier Hicks of Nova Scotia, who was keenly aware of the serious problem in the coal industry, and his initial overtures were of course followed up by officials of Dosco and the dominion coal board.


It is sometimes said there is no market for Nova Scotia coal in central Canada, but when you speak about any market at the same time you have to speak about the price at which this coal can be sold in the central Canadian market. I illustrate this point by reference to the fact that there is a market with two large consumers for 800,000 tons of coal between lake Erie and lake Huron. I am not saying it is the only market, but there is a market of that magnitude with two consumers in that area, and apparently Nova Scotia coal meets the requirements of those particular consumers. But in order to dispose of that Nova Scotia coal it would require a subvention rate of $8 per ton to make the coal competitive with United States coal. As you know, at present the maximum subvention rate is $4.75 a ton, and is costing approximately $8 million a year.
I believe that most serious Nova Scotians are resigned to the fact that there is a limit beyond which this subvention cannot be increased. It seems the most sensible course is to anticipate a gradual decline in the production costs of coal. On two previous occasions in the house I put forward the view that there were untapped productive contributions within the work force itself. My views on the subject were supported by the experience of No. 1-B colliery this spring. Before the announcement of closure of this colliery, daily production was running about 1,400 tons. When the company gave notice to the provincial government that it proposed to close the colliery because of high costs of production, daily production increased to 1,800 tons, and I am informed that it reached and may have even exceeded a daily rate of production of 2,000 tons.
I think it is important to point out that this rather significant decrease in production costs occurred without any change in mining conditions, without any change in the number of the work force, and without any new managerial practices. I am told that the result of this increase in daily production was to reduce the cost of producing coal in that colliery by $2 per ton. This rise in daily output and the accompanying decrease in production costs represents in my mind a change of attitude or a real stimulus provided to these coal miners by the threat of closure. If this outcome were possible under these precarious and unstable conditions, then I should like to ask what could we expect to have if this problem of production were tackled on a wider basis, and if there were brought into play an organized and intelligent approach to the question of human motivation and the problem of labour-management relations?

This phase of the problem was touched upon at the recent convention of united mine workers at Truro by one of the miner delegates, who was reported in the press as having said that management must so arrange things that its employees will have the will to work. I think it would be a mistake to put this expression "will to work" in the narrow context of greater physical effort. It means much more than this. It embraces a cooperative approach in the field of labour-management relations and the setting up of organized channels by which the work force can contribute ideas as well as muscles to the productive efforts of the Cape Breton coal mines.
Because I have advocated this type of labour-management co-operative endeavour as a partial solution to the problem of the high costs of the Nova Scotia coal industry, I want to bring this illustration before the house to remind members that there is something within the human attitudes of the Cape Breton coal mine miners that if properly brought into play can tackle the problem of production much more quickly and more efficiently than any type of machinery or mechanization.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was speaking about the improvement in productivity that had occurred in No. 1-B colliery shortly after the announcement of its imminent closing. I pointed out at that time that this improvement in productivity had occurred without any increase in the number of personnel, or any change in managerial techniques, or any change in the physical conditions of mining. I went on to point out that this development should be an example of the type of labour-management approach to the problem of productivity in coal mines generally in Cape Breton island.
I believe that at present a basis exists for this type of approach. The executive of the U.M.W. has shown a completely responsible attitude in this situation. Last year the executive was endorsed by the rank and file in maintaining the existing wage contracts in so far as increases were concerned. In addition to that in certain collieries, including No. 1-B, pit committees were organized in an effort to use the productive knowledge of experienced miners. I believe this responsible approach should be extended and
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys developed on a broad front, which would be a new productive relationship in the collieries of the Cape Breton coal industry.
I want to say a word, Mr. Chairman, about the subvention policy, because the continuation of this policy is so essential to the welfare of the coal industry. As is well known, the subvention is a transportation subsidy for the movement of Canadian coal to make it competitive with the United States product. It seems pretty clear that this subvention, in its origin, was an adaptation to the coal industry of the national policy of tariff protection. It was clear that a protective tariff could not be applied to the Canadian coal industry because Canadian production could not satisfy Canadian coal requirements in full, unless we were prepared to accept a highly uneconomical operation of certain Canadian coal mines. The subvention was therefore introduced in order to guarantee markets for Canadian coal in certain parts of Canada and, at the same time, maintain a suitable level of employment in the coal mines of Canada.
It seems also clear, if an examination is made of the origin of this subvention, that it was really a quid pro quo given to the Nova Scotians, or the extreme end of the country, as a substitute for tariff protection that could not easily be applied. Viewed in that light, in my judgment the subvention is not only a commitment to sustain a certain level of production in the coal industry, but also represents a commitment to sustain a certain level of employment in the industries in the extremities of the country. At present, however, especially having regard to the importing of residual oil, the subvention is becoming less adequate as an instrument for maintaining this industry.
At the present time the future of the coal industry in Nova Scotia is not very bright. It is asserted that by 1957 the Canadian National Railways will be using no Nova Scotia coal, and as has been pointed out by other hon. members there are sources of competition. I think Nova Scotians generally will be compelled to fight vigorously for the survival of this industry. If the economy of Nova Scotia were developing on other fronts, if other industrial opportunities were opening up, then we could face the prospect of a decline in the coal industry because what we lost in coal would be made up in development elsewhere. This, of course, is not true of the present state of the Nova Scotia economy. It is quite all right to suggest in general that workers move from a declining industry into an expanding industry. Indeed, such a transfer is sometimes argued, and properly so, as eventually contributing more to productivity and human welfare.
6754	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
However, the coal industry is the basis of the industrial economy of the whole province, and a transfer could only occur from Nova Scotia to other parts of Canada. Such a solution to the problem of the Nova Scotia coal industry fails to take into account the real social and political problems that are involved. I used the word "political" in the widest possible sense. I think it should be pointed out also that if we agree that the economy of all Nova Scotia is dependent upon the coal industry, the economy of the eastern section of Nova Scotia is even more vitally dependent upon this industry. At the time we are facing this crisis in the coal industry in eastern Nova Scotia we are faced with adversity in three communities that are now in a very precarious position as a result of the changes brought about by the construction of the Canso causeway, in which project both federal and provincial governments have interests and commitments.
I would think, sir, the wise course for both the federal and provincial governments would be to start consideration of the alternatives that could be provided to build up the economy of Nova Scotia. I believe the problems confronting the eastern end of the province arising from the coal industry and the Canso project should be a proper area for the joint resources planning of the federal and provincial governments.
A very interesting project, in so far as the island of Cape Breton was concerned, was completed some months ago with the announcement of the results of the joint inventory of the forest resources of Nova Scotia. This inventory was initiated by this government and the resources, in so far as the island of Cape Breton is concerned, are very promising. It has now been confirmed that there exist in this part of Nova Scotia ample sources of supply for the requirements of a rather large pulp and paper plant.
At the same time it is also becoming evident that there are very interesting mineral indications in the Cape Breton Highlands national park. At the moment this area of the province is closed to development, because its terrain is used for recreational purposes.
Last summer I understand the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys had two survey parties within the confines of the park in an effort to verify these interesting mineral indications. I do not know what the results of these surveys have been or will be, but I think they will serve to confirm what has already been determined by private prospectors; that there are, in that area of Cape Breton, mineral deposits of commercial proportions. Because of these factors we are not completely at a loss with respect to


alternative sources or alternative methods of economic development in the eastern area of Nova Scotia. But because the federal government is committed, through its various policies, to the coal industry; and because the provincial government is committed to the same industry because of its control over natural resources, it seems to me this would be a very suitable time for some co-ordinated effort to be made by the federal and provincial governments to explore further the prospects of forest and mineral development in this part of Nova Scotia.
I think if we allow ourselves to be deluded into believing that the problems of the coal industry will be solved within a short time, we are not facing the facts as they have been outlined by other speakers this afternoon. And may I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that both the federal and provincial governments make a real start soon at what X would call joint regional or area economic development, by trying to co-ordinate efforts to develop the forest wealth of eastern Nova Scotia and the mineral deposits to be found within the confines of Cape Breton Highlands national park.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in opening my remarks I should like first to compliment the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys upon the statement he gave this afternoon at the beginning of this discussion. I do not compliment him because he painted a cheerful picture, although on the other hand I should like to say that the hon. gentleman off to my left somewhere, who apparently considered the minister's statement as a sort of funeral oration, very considerably mistook its import. But I do think the minister gave us a plain, unvarnished and undistorted statement of the conditions facing the Canadian coal industry today.
Mr. Chairman, there is one thing we cannot afford, and that is to adopt a spirit of false complacency with regard to this matter. I say that with some conviction, because recently I have been studying the report of the dominion coal board for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955, with, so far as I was concerned, particular reference to the present state and the future prospects of the Nova Scotia coal industry. These annual reports, I may say, always command the close attention of all those hon. members who, like myself, represent constituencies in which the mining of coal is a very important element of industrial activity, for the role of this federal agency in respect of the Canadian coal industry is a weighty one and is likely to become more so.
Although this latest report is not entirely without encouraging features, and although

during the year the Nova Scotia coal mining industry as a whole actually increased production over the previous year, yet I do not see anything in that report which can in any way encourage a spirit of easy optimism in my part of the country. And even if the report were more cheering than it actually is, certainly we in Nova Scotia would have very great difficulty in persuading ourselves into any such spirit of optimism. Events in our province during past months and the past year-the closing of some mines; slack times in other mines, the whole climaxed by the closing of No. 1-B colliery at Glace Bay, Cape Breton-all these are things which confirm only too clearly that our Nova Scotia coal industry is passing through a period of uncertainty and even of crisis. Therefore I think it fitting at this time once again to draw to the attention of the house the importance of the Nova Scotia coal mining industry to the whole economy of the province.
I realize that in all I am saying, possibly to a large extent in everything I shall say, I shall be repeating what other speakers before me have said both this afternoon and this evening. Nevertheless I think these are matters which bear repetition. They should be driven home with the utmost emphasis.
For some years we have seen the coal situation progressively deteriorating. It has been forecast repeatedly that by the middle sixties, about ten years from now, increased population and industrial activity throughout Canada will again, in spite of the competition from other fuels, arrest this decline in the coal industry and raise the demand for coal to a level sufficient to ensure the continuing operation of our mines on at least their present scale.
We may still hope that prophecy will prove ultimately correct. Nor, I think, with all deference to atomic power or any other developments, is there as yet any real indication that in the foreseeable future coal will cease to be a major source of energy in this country. But as we read the latest reports of the dominion coal board, to which I have just referred, we in Nova Scotia find the outlook for the immediate future summed up in one ominous sentence: "The markets for Nova Scotia coal are in a dangerous condition".
Therefore it behooves us to remember that ten years can be a long time in the history of an industry; and if we simply wait for a general expansion of Canadian population and industrial activity over a decade-inevitable though I believe such expansion to be-to rectify the coal situation, coal mining in the meantime may diminish to an extent such as to render it impossible to revive to a point
25. 1955	G755
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys even approaching its present level. Unfortunately collieries, like coffin lids, tend to close with a very considerable degree of finality.
Let me therefore emphasize again that to Nova Scotia the loss or the extensive curtailment of our coal industry must constitute a staggering blow to our entire economy. Often enough-too often-in the past we have lost individual enterprises, perhaps a factory here or a factory there, and in time made good the loss, at whatever cost of temporary dislocation and hardship. But there is no form of industrial or other economic activity at present foreseeable in Nova Scotia with which we can hope in any real, adequate measure to replace a vanished or drastically curtailed coal industry.
Carried to its fullest extent, such a catastrophe would affect directly perhaps a fifth of our population, and certainly the ramifications would extend in some degree to nearly every segment of the remainder. First and foremost' to be considered, of course, is the miner thrown out of work, as were several hundred of them when No. 1-B colliery at Glace Bay was closed. This of course includes the miner and his dependents. But the consequences would reach infinitely farther, and include the merchant whose customers can no longer buy, the farmer whose market for his produce shrinks, the lumberman whose sale of pitprops becomes a thing of the past. Yes, Mr. Chairman, so far would the consequences reach that it is hardly an exaggeration to say that the loss or further serious curtailment of our Nova Scotia coal industry would be felt in one way or another by every resident of the province. I have said that our primary concern must be for the miner himself and his dependents. I think that is the view of every member in the house. To any man the loss of his means of livelihood is a disaster, and that is particularly so when it means that no longer can he follow the occupation in which perhaps most of his productive years have been spent.
Coal mining is, I know, beset by the same difficulties in western Canada as it is in the east, and I certainly do not wish to be accused of minimizing the seriousness of the situation anywhere. But I think it is not unfair to say that in the west the shock of the decline of the industry has at least been cushioned by the ability to absorb many of its displaced workers into an otherwise soaring economy; perhaps, ironically enough, into those very oil and natural gas developments which have played so striking a part in the enfeeblement of the coal industry.
On the Atlantic seaboard the opportunities for the displaced coal miner to shift to other

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys local forms of employment exist in no comparable degree. Although we are not without promising prospects of future expansion in several of our basic economic pursuits such as fishing, lumbering and the mining of base metals, to name a few, there can be no sure or immediate hope that any large numbers of personnel displaced from the collieries can be readily absorbed into other phases of the industrial life of the areas concerned.
What, then, is the alternative? Is it to be migration to other, distant regions of Canada? If that is to be the remedy, it is one that must carry with it dire consequences; the depopulation of long-settled communities, the abandonment of established homes, the breaking of family and other social ties, hardship and distress to individuals, and certainly an appalling economic loss to the province of Nova Scotia.
Much, it is true, might be done for many individuals under such circumstances by the inauguration of an extensive program of retraining to refit them for other trades and callings; and certainly I cannot urge too strongly the importance of providing all facilities necessary for the purpose of carrying on such a program to whatever extent may from time to time be required. If, indeed, by such retraining all or most of the displaced coal miners could be taken again into the industrial fabric in the areas where they have lived, or even in other parts of Nova Scotia, we in that province could face with considerably more equanimity the prospect of a further decline in employment in our collieries. But, as I have said, the possibility of any such extensive absorption is certainly not promising. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, no program of retraining or rehabilitation, thought it would certainly prove of inestimable value in many individual cases, could be considered as more than a secondary remedy, one which necessarily would fall far short of providing a complete answer to the whole situation.
That complete answer, that primary remedy, if I may call it that, can be found only through the united efforts and co-operation of all those concerned-management and labour, whose responsibility it is to reach and maintain the utmost possible peak of efficiency in production, the provincial government, this government-through their united efforts and co-operation, to continue the Nova Scotia coal industry on at least an approximation of its present level through the years immediately ahead, until such time as the inevitable expansion of Canadian population and industrial activity, aided, we hope, by such developments as the coal-fired

gas turbine engine and the successful economic adaptation of coal to uses other than as fuel, may place the industry again in a sound condition.
Although, as I have suggested, management and labour have a fundamental role in the attainment and maintenance of the maximum possible degree of efficiency in production-and that is certainly an essential, as was pointed out just a few minutes ago-and although management has the primary responsibility to find sales outlets, yet it is, of course, self-evident that in the present state of the industry a considerable degree of governmental assistance is also a requisite. In this chamber we are chiefly concerned with the nature and extent of the assistance furnished by the federal government.
I do not wish at this time to dwell upon all the various ways in which the government renders assistance to the Nova Scotia coal industry, but I should like to make some very short comments upon that form which normally, perhaps, one thinks of first, namely, subventions. The importance of that assistance is shown by the fact that in the last fiscal year over $8,500,000 were expended in subventions to aid the movement of Nova Scotia coal to markets, an increase of more than $1,500,000 over the previous fiscal year. I think the minister gave the exact figure. This government is also to be highly commended upon its recent decision to extend this form of assistance, on an experimental basis, it is true, to overseas shipments in the hope of thereby enabling Nova Scotia coal to find new outlets in Britain and Germany.
I note that in its latest report the dominion coal board refers to high subventions as an unhealthy factor in the coal situation. True as that statement is from many points of view-and certainly it would be infinitely preferable to have no need for such assistance -I should like to emphasize that the loss or further drastic decline of the Nova Scotia coal industry would inevitably precipitate a far more unhealthy condition. Certainly I think the corpse of a dead coal industry would poison the entire lifestream of our province.
In passing, I should like to say that the government is also to be commended upon the 10 per cent preference in cost which it has afforded to Canadian coal as against other coal for use in coal-burning government installations. The minister mentioned that item this afternoon.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have been dwelling intentionally, yet I do not think unduly, upon the dark aspects of the situation. I am glad to note from the report of the dominion coal

board and from other quarters that, apart altogether from long-term possibilities, there are a number of encouraging factors also. The upswing of general industrial activity even now materializing under the beneficent trade and fiscal policies of this government, the stiffened fight to retain the domestic market for coal, the prospects of greater use of coal in the maritimes for the generation of electricity by steam, as outlined in the Christie report, the news which indicates that the perfection of the coal-fired gas turbine locomotive-and with it the regaining of lost outlets for coal-may be far nearer than we had thought; all such matters brighten somewhat a generally sombre picture.
I am not unmindful of the fact that the minister mentioned the other day, and repeated today, that the turbine is still in the experimental stage; but still the news indicates the possibility of the imminent perfection of the coal-fired gas turbine locomotive. But, as I said before, it will require the united efforts of all concerned, the intelligent combination and exploitation to the full of every favourable factor, to preserve the Nova Scotia coal industry from further decay. It is my hope that this government will continue to take a leading part in endeavouring to bring about an efficient correlation of all those efforts into a comprehensive plan, including, I may add, the study of every feasible means of formulating a workable energy policy for the country, which the dominion coal board calls a necessity for any long-term solution of coal problems.
With reference to the whole subject, and the matter of continued government assistance to the coal industry, I should like, Mr. Chairman, to close by quoting one more statement from the latest report of the board:
It is to be remembered that the Canadian coal industry is basic and one upon which our economy is still largely dependent.
Implicit in such a statement, Mr. Chairman, is the truth that the preservation of the Canadian coal industry is a matter not merely of local or provincial, but of national, concern.

I wish to thank hon. members who have spoken, for their constructive speeches. I agree with most hon. members who have spoken that the coal industry is in a precarious position. It is difficult to be optimistic about the future of the industry. But the very fact that members on all sides of the house, the unions, the companies concerned, the provincial governments and the federal government are really facing the hard, cold facts of the situation is a hopeful sign.

I believe a great deal can be done to reduce the cost of production although I cannot put my finger on just where the trouble is. I sometimes think the force of circumstances will be more effective in bringing about improvement in production than good intentions have been in the past. The industry is certainly facing a battle for survival, and I believe that now more than ever before everyone realizes that they have a responsibility.
The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond made some very good suggestions and I do hope that the industry will be able to implement some of them. I believe that in the field of human relations, employer-employee relations if you will, there is room for improvement. I have been down through the mines in Nova Scotia; I have been in the wash houses when the men came off shift, and
[Mr. Prudham.l

I have been underground, and I must say that you cannot find a more honest and conscientious group of workmen anywhere. I have been associated with management, and I know that some of these men are actually working themselves into their graves. I can think of one or two who will have to slow up if they are going to be much use to the industry for much longer. I believe that all the way through these people are sincere; nevertheless there is room for closer co-operation, and I think we would all be surprised at the result if some of the suggestions made here this evening were carried out.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned the need for an energy committee in Canada. We have that now within the government. It was started about a year ago. They have had several meetings. The committee consists of representatives of the various departments concerned with energy development or the use of energy in various forms: national defence, the defence research board, the Department of Transport, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Labour. All have key men on that so-called energy committee.
True, we have not the powers my hon. friend thinks would probably be necessary to direct this development of energy in Canada, but he himself said earlier in his speech that we must not forget that the responsibility for the development of resources rests primarily with the provinces. In turn the provinces let out the development of those resources to companies and individuals. Unless this parliament is prepared to give tremendous powers to some minister or some board. I do not think we could direct the industry. We can do it in an educational way. We can gather the information and present it to the people concerned and try to direct it in that way, but we cannot push people around. I forgot to say the dominion coal board is represented on that committee. The chairman of the coal board is the chairman of the committee.
The hon. member for Lethbridge still has his eye on the Ontario market for domestic coal from his area. I do not propose to go into that in detail. One thing to remember is that our western domestic coal will not store well. It has to be delivered when the customer wants it, and there is sometimes difficulty in bringing about that arrangement.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo referred to the high cost of coal in Newfoundland. I do not know where the responsibility lies. He suggests that the Dominion Coal Company is largely responsible, but I have

the idea that probably the people in Newfoundland handle the distribution of their coal and have dealers there. I have been told by people who claim to know the situation that there is quite a bit of difficulty in the various ports in having that coal handled economically. Various interests and unions are concerned. Someone told me while I was in Nova Scotia last week that in some ports the port officials or the union, I do not know which, insist that the coal be unloaded in very small buckets in the way it was done perhaps 50 years ago. If modern equipment were installed the cost could be greatly reduced.
His suggestions were good, and I hope everyone concerned has a very close look at the Newfoundland situation. We are not extending subvention assistance this year to coal moving to Newfoundland because we do not think it is necessary. We think that market can be held by the Nova Scotia coal industry without assistance. If it cannot there is something wrong, because it is their natural market.
The hon. member who has just spoken made some very constructive suggestions. I shall not take the time of the house now to make any further comments, except in reference to one thing the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned. He paid a compliment to the present officials of the coal board and to the minister for the way the problem is being handled at the present time. I wish to thank him for those compliments, but I did not like his reference to officials and ministers who have gone before. I think that was hardly fair. Although I have been associated with this industry for only a few years, I know that many people have conscientiously struggled with this problem before. I have here an extract from a book that was written by Dr. Charles Camsell, a former deputy minister of mines. He was also chairman of the dominion fuel board at one time. It reads:
The dominion fuel board, another of my responsibilities from its creation, was always a headache. It was a very necessary board, because of the unfortunate location of our coal fields relative to the great consuming centres of the country and the concentration of our population in the coal-less areas. The difficulty of overcoming the handicap of geography is illustrated more acutely in our fuel problem than in any other field of domestic economic relations. The problem of coal still remains, and indeed seems to become more acute as time goes on. There is not a great deal that can be done about it, because geography refuses to be changed.
Those are the words of a man who struggled with this problem years ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
He did not struggle very much. He just blamed it on geography.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Anyway, the subvention policy has been followed by this government and other governments for almost 30 years. One of the officials here this evening mentioned that when United States coal was being sold for 90 cents at the lake ports, a subvention was provided to make Nova Scotia coal competitive with that 90 cent coal at that time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to assure the minister that I was not casting any reflections on past administrators. I said it was the first time since I had been in the house that the problem was really taken hold of and the minister was making an attempt to at least understand it. For the last 16 years, all during the war period and until a few years ago, we did not have to sell coal. It was a problem of finding coal. But in the last four or five years we have been getting back into a peacetime economy where we have to sell coal, and we are getting into difficulty.
I should like to ask the minister a few questions while I am on my feet. First I want to straighten the record as between myself and the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. When the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond was making his analysis of the closing of No. 1-B colliery, he stated that when the coal conference took place in Halifax the cost factor was the one that was stressed in regard to that colliery, but even if that cost factor had not been there at all there still would have been no market for the coal produced in that colliery. That was in contradiction to what the minister said in his statement, and I agree with the minister. The minister stated that there was a market in the Canadian National Railways for the product of that mine if they could give them the quality of coal they required. I just wanted to straighten out that particular point, because it is an important one.
The second question I should like to ask the minister is this. He stated that the board was not in a position to give us the names of the operators of the Dominion Import Company or, to a large extent, the amount of coal they imported. That is rather strange, because I understand the federal government has to issue a permit to that company to import coal from the United States. That permit naturally would have to set out the personnel of the company. Does the minister still insist he does not know the names of the people who form that company, and whether it is a subsidiary of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Investigation by the coal board establishes, I believe, that it is not a subsidiary of the Dominion Coal Company,
6760	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys although there might be one man who is on both boards. To the best of the knowledge of the coal board no permit is necessary for the importation of coal. We have records of all movements of coal where a subvention is involved, but so far as other movements are concerned we do not get the details of the operations of various companies. We have the total through examining the customs clearances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: It is a rather strange set-up that anybody can start an importing company on his own and just notify the government board that he is entitled to certain drawbacks, particularly when he gets a drawback of 49 cents out of a duty of 50 cents on metallurgical coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Is that not what the minister said, that it is not necessary for anyone to get a permit in order to go into the business of importing coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: They do not get any assistance in any form from this government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Does the Dominion Import Company in Montreal get any assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: None whatever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
What I have in my mind, Mr. Chairman, is that two years ago I saw a photostatic copy of an advertisement of the Dominion Coal Company advertising the sale of Kentucky coal in the province of Ontario. That advertisement was signed by the Dominion Coal Company. Therefore, it is my assumption that if there is not a chartered import company, the Dominion Coal Company as such must be in the import business themselves. The statement I made on the subject which the minister attributed to me was actually read from the report of the royal commission under Mr. Justice W. F. Carroll in 1946, setting out the position that the Dominion Coal Company had imported approximately 2 million tons of coal and marketed it in the province of Ontario, which was the normal market under subventions for Nova Scotia coal previous to the war.
I want to get that matter straightened out, because I have no doubt in my own mind that this particular organization imported coal in 1944 and marketed it in central Canada, and that the same thing is still being carried on whether they are doing it by the back door or by the front door.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: We do not know of any Dominion Import Company. There is a Canadian Import Company. I believe that is the one the hon. member has in mind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: As I understand it, until about the end of last year this is the way the Dominion Coal Company operated. They have a salesman who goes out in November and starts to take orders for next year. He sells all the coal he can, and in recent years he has sometimes sold more coal than the Dominion Coal Company was able to produce. In order to hold the business he had to supply coal to satisfy the sales he had made. I am told by officials of the Dominion Coal Company, and I have to take their word for it, that at no time has any imported coal replaced one pound of Nova Scotia production. I believe them when they say that. I believe the union when they tell me sincerely what they have to say. I have no reason to disbelieve what the company says, and I think that is a fact.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Well, I do not believe it. We had a market for about 2 million tons of coal in the province of Ontario in 1939 and 1940, and I think that is the normal market for Nova Scotia coal under the present subvention arrangement. I know the fight that was put up to build up the subventions. It was started, mind you, by Hon. Gordon Harrington under a Conservative government in Nova Scotia. There was a struggle to build up the subventions to a point where we could get at least 2 million tons of coal into that market. We succeeded in doing that. I had no objection to the company trying to hold their customers in that area during the war when our coal was diverted to other uses.
I talked to the general manager of the Dominion Coal Company in 1940 for a whole evening on this particular subject. He told me what they were doing, and I reminded him not to forget that we did the same thing from 1914 to 1918 and lost the Montreal market. I pointed out the difficulties and struggles we had to regain that market, and told him not to forget that if they were relinquishing the Ontario market they should only do so under some agreement that the market would be returned to Nova Scotia when the war was over. That man passed away later, and I have no doubt that if he had been alive we would not be arguing about this matter today. I believe these people intended that that was what should be done.
We are not going to settle the matter tonight, but I still maintain that there is a market for Nova Scotia coal in the Canadian National Railways if the Dominion Coal

Company can supply the grade of coal required. I say that regardless of the question of cost, and the improvement of the product is their job.
I should like to ask the minister another question. Let us settle this business of the coal-fired turbine engine. That has been tossed around for two years now as something that was going to solve all the problems. The pathetic part of that kind of propaganda is that when you have a thousand people whose means of livelihood depends on that industry and something like that comes out in the headlines in the newspapers, they get the idea that there is some hope. But they get a shock a year later when nothing happens.
I should like the minister to put his official opinion on the record, and he knows the situation, with respect to whether he thinks that in the foreseeable future the coal-fired turbine may be an instrument that can be used on the railroads of Canada and which will restore the markets for coal in the railways. How long does the minister think it is going to be before that takes place? Would he also clarify the point whether the present engine, if and when it is perfected, can be substituted in diesel units now in operation? If a locomotive has a diesel engine, can that engine be exchanged for a turbine engine if and when the turbine is perfected?
I ask that question because I have an editorial in my hand taken from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, a very responsible newspaper. If you read the editorial it would lead you to believe that all that stands between the development of the coal-fired turbine engine and the restoration of the market for coal on the national railways is $1 million, and that if somebody can find $1 million they can put it on the rails. I think it is pretty nearly time some sanity was brought into the thinking on this subject, and I should like to have an official statement from the people who know.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
The hon. member has given me a big order. The coal-fired turbine is definitely an experiment. I know that for several years the men of our fuels division, Professor Mordell of McGill University, Mr. Forsyth of the Dominion Coal Company and others have thought it shows a great deal of promise. We must not forget that it took 50 years to develop the diesel engine to its present state of perfection. We do not have an engine yet. We just have an experimental unit that shows promise. It was put into operation some months ago, and it ran very well. However, certain weaknesses showed up and they thought it was better to tear the machine down to correct those defects before the tests had been carried through to 50433-427
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys completion and in order that more accurate data could be supplied to a locomotive company or some other private industry that might be interested in the development of a prototype engine.
I am not going to stick my neck out and say how soon it will become a practical engine. I do not know whether it will interchange with diesels, but I believe that is what they have in mind, that it would fit a conventional chassis. The Nova Scotia government had their men keep a very close eye on it, and they even intimated that at the right time they might consider spending some money on this development. So far as this department is concerned, we are presently only going to carry it through the experimental stage. The actual, practical application of the machine will have to be considered at another time. At the moment we are doing everything we can to carry it through this period to see if it really has merit and to see what, if any, value it will have from the standpoint of saving fuel or what value it will be to the coal industry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
While we are on the subject, I have a clipping in my hand here from one of the local newspapers. It was published within the last couple of days and this is the headline: "Claim coal dust runs locomotive." This could be a good way of getting rid of a lot of the dust we have in Nova Scotia. The dateline is Berlin:
An East German state-owned factory at Potsdam has completed the first locomotive to be driven with coal dust, the communist East German news agency ADN reported Sunday. The agency said the locomotive could reach a speed of about 60 miles an hour while pulling 600 tons weight, and do a 300-mile journey on 18-5 tons of coal dust.
Well now, is the coal board familiar with any such development? You know, we are getting a high percentage of slack and the difficulty is in selling our slack. I would be interested in finding out just what kind of engine they are operating in that particular locomotive; or is it just propaganda?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: We sent one of our scientists from the fuels division to Europe last year to observe any work that was being done on coal beneficiation or the development of engines, etc. He did not tell me about that one. We will have to look into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
There is another matter I should like to get straightened out, and the Minister of Public Works is connected with this one. During the consideration of public works estimates he was questioned by an hon. member as to why, in a new public building in Woodstock, New Brunswick, the coal board had recommended against the use of coal as a fuel. I was rather surprised to hear that
6762	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the coal board would do that kind of thing. The Minister of Public Works was going to get me the answer, because I said there must be some pretty broad considerations if the coal board considered making that kind of recommendation to the minister. Before the minister could get me the answer his estimates were completed, and I think perhaps this would be a good time to ask the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to tell us if that is correct. I believe there would have to be consultation with public works in regard to the fuel needs in regard to the building, and why would they recommend oil as against coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Before my colleague answers that, I think I should correct a wrong impression. It was not the fuel board that recommended we should use oil instead of coal. We discussed this with the coal board and on the information that developed we thought oil should be used. It is the responsibility of our officials.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: On the recommendation of the coal board.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: No, not upon the recommendation but on the strength of the facts that developed from the study by the board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I was rather startled when I heard the Minister of Public Works say that on the recommendation of the coal board-it is in Hansard-this was done. The minister would have to take responsibility for the type of equipment installed, but I got the impression from the minister that, since the building was designed for oil, in consultation with the coal board and upon the recommendation of the coal board it was decided that the design of the building should not be changed for heating purposes, and that oil should be used. In effect it was a recommendation against the use of coal in a building in the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I think I can throw a little more light on that. For a number of years there has been an interdepartmental committee which reviewed fuel problems for the Department of National Defence. This committee made a careful assessment of national defence installations and advised the national defence department of their findings in accordance with the government's fuel policy. The final decision, of course, was left with the Department of National Defence. On March 8, 1955, there was a cabinet directive that stated that before fuel-burning equipment in any government building or building under government control which consumed 500 tons of coal per year or more was changed from coal to other fuel, the department concerned would consult with


the dominion coal board or the interdepartmental fuel committee on the cost of the various fuels and other relative factors.
This committee started to function almost immediately after the cabinet directive, and the question of the fuel in the Woodstock building was one of the first items that came before it. It came before the committee on May 20. I understand that prior to that meeting officers of the Department of Public Works had carried out a study of the relative costs of fuel for that building on their own, and according to their calculations there was quite a large saving by installing oil-burning equipment. Before the new committee set up under the cabinet directive began to function, that oil-burning equipment had already been installed. Although they were able to show that there possibly was not as large a saving by burning oil, it was considered that since the equipment was already installed it should be left there.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I just want to make sure there is no onus on the coal board for that decision. The statement I made appears in Hansard at page 6392, July 19, 1955, and reads as follows:
It is an oil heating system. We considered coal, and took the problem to the coal board to obtain their views. We came to the conclusion that the differential was such that we should go along with the oil installation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
The minister was reading from the wrong page. The question I asked him is at page 6395, and reads as follows:
I should like the minister to clarify something he said a few minutes ago in his exchange with the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton when referring to the new public building at Woodstock. Did I understand the minister to say that this building was being heated by oil on the advice of the dominion coal board?
The minister's answer was as follows:
No. Perhaps I did give a wrong impression. It is the policy of the government to check the heating systems of all public buildings with the coal board and unless the economics of the situation are pretty compelling we lean towards the use of coal.
That is a policy which any maritimer would support at this stage. In this instance the building was designed to be heated by oil and after the system was installed the matter was brought to the attention of the officials and we asked the coal board to study the problem to decide whether or not a change should be made. After a study was made of all aspects of the problem a conclusion was reached that a change should not be made from oil to coal.
That is exactly what the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys has said. Then I said:
Of course the minister's department did what I think should have been done, but we might as well clear up what were the economics of the situation. What were the reasons why the coal board, which is set up and designed to secure coal markets and that kind of thing, made a decision like that?

Then the Minister of Public Works said he would get the information. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys clarified the situation to this extent, that while there was interdepartmental consultation the committee had changed, and the Minister of Public Works installed oil-burning equipment. Naturally when the coal board was referred to again they said, "To tear it all out and put in other equipment would create some further compelling economic factors." But I think there was something wrong with the view taken by the Minister of Public Works in the beginning. With this coal controversy, and the shortage of markets, they designed a building to burn oil in the maritime provinces, and within 60 miles of Minto coal. I think the minister's department should come in for some castigation in that instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The information is now en route to the hon. member. He will be able to judge for himself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have no extended remarks, but there are two or three questions I should like to ask before the item carries. I should like to know whether the minister has readily available any figures on the current annual production rate of coal on Vancouver island, and whether in that connection he has any contrasting figures from five or ten years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: We have figures for British Columbia as a whole, but not the island alone.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I should have liked that information. It has been suggested to me that the current annual production rate is running at something like 900 tons a month, as contrasted with 9,000 tons a month not many years ago. Perhaps those figures are close enough for the purpose I have in mind.
As the minister probably knows, that reduction in annual production is not because there is not more coal on Vancouver island. My understanding is that there are still substantial reserves of it. A year or two ago it was suggested to me by someone in the power production field, someone whom I considered v/ell qualified to speak, that it might not be too long until on Vancouver island, having reached the limit of our available hydro sources, once again we might be turning to the use of coal for power purposes.
For certain reasons I find myself interested in some of the references made to the possibility of the use of coal for power in the mari-times, because some day we may be able to take advantage of that experience on Vancouver island.
In that same connection I recall that during the meeting of the standing committee on external affairs earlier this year, when we 50433-427J
25, 1955	6763
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys had as a witness General A. G. L. McNaughton, chairman of the international joint commission, he made some reference to power development by steam. His reference is found at page 101 of the proceedings of the committee. The general, of course, was referring to the value of downstream benefits of water released under regulated flow. But he does state here with reference to the lower Columbia basin that-
-the newest and latest in pressure steam plants being built in the basin, the best one on tide water, running at base load, will cost 51 mills per kilowatt hour at the bus bars.
He goes on to say that some in a little less favourable position are producing power at about 6 mills. I wonder if the minister can give us any idea whether steam power is being produced in Nova Scotia or other areas of the maritime provinces today at any figure that compares favourably with or approaches the ones I have mentioned. If not, what steps are being taken by the coal board, or any other federal agencies, to encourage the production of power at those rates in the maritime areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
It is perhaps beyond the terms of reference of the coal board to make studies of comparative costs of power production. But in order to assist the industry in Nova Scotia a year ago we engaged the services of Dr. Christie to make a very thorough and comprehensive study of power development in the maritimes area. His reports were turned over to the provincial governments, in the hope that they would be assisted in their efforts to produce cheaper power from coal. Copies of those reports are available to hon. members who wish to have them.
We are assisting in the experimental development of the coal-fired turbine, which possibly can be adaptable to power production. I did not hear the hydro costs the hon. member mentioned, but it would not mean much anyway. I do not think coal-fired power plants can compete with hydro in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: In order to produce cheap power you must have cheap coal. That is something they do not have on Vancouver island or in Nova Scotia. If I remember correctly the power plant in the city of Edmonton, which formerly burned coal, now burns gas and produces electricity at somewhere around 5 mills. I think they paid about $3 a ton for the coal. When you compare that with the cost of coal in Nova Scotia or on Vancouver island, of somewhere around $9 a ton-it approximates that, anyway-you are a long way from producing cheap power with that high-cost coal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I went over the Christie report carefully. A year ago I had a discussion on this subject with the general manager of the steel company at Sydney, Mr. Anson. The steel company operates a large thermo-power plant from the town of Glace Bay, which pretty well supplies the needs of the industrial areas of the island. They are extending the whole line up toward the strait of Canso. You can burn splint or anything else that will burn in one of those thermo-power plants. Mr. Anson told me that at that large plant in Glace Bay, which is close to the mining communities, they were putting power on the site far cheaper than any hydroelectric power company in Canada could do it. If we were successful in attracting any industry into that area to ease the unemployment problem, they could and would sell power to any industry that might come in there cheaper than they could buy it anywhere else in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Good.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I had that from the general manager of the steel company. They are producing that power from coal that is produced in the area, which the minister considers very high-cost coal. Mind you, you can use a lot of the waste by pulverizing it, and that sort of thing. There is no shortage
LMr. Barnett.]
of power in that particular area. The impression has gone abroad that there may be, but there is not; and it is cheap power. It is available. I wanted to say that because it is only a short time ago since I talked to that man about it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I understood the Calgary Power and Light company-I believe that is the name-in Calgary were going to put a thermoelectric plant at Wabamun. I think by burning coal they were able to compete with their own hydro power from the river at Calgary.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, they are going to burn gas, I understand, for the first 10 years, but that plant will be sitting right on a coal bed. The cost of the coal is the cost of stripping it, $1.50, $2, or somewhere around that figure. Maybe it will go to $3 a ton, but it is very cheap coal. I believe they will be able to produce cheap power under those circumstances. Another power plant is being built in Alberta at Forestburg, where strip coal is very cheap. I have heard of that coal having been sold in trainload lots to get rid of the surplus at about 60 cents a ton. Although I do not think they could survive at that price, they do sell it as low as that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: If I noted correctly one of the statements the minister made earlier today, he said that at the present time gas is a cheaper source of synthetics than coal. In view of that statement can the minister tell us what research projects the government has initiated to discover how cheaper synthetics can be produced from coal at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Some years ago the department of mines started on a co-operative project with the United States bureau of mines. It was agreed at that time that the United States would carry on the study of coal if our department would undertake the study of bitumen. In view of the fact that we have the Athabasca tar sands in this country, we set up a high-pressure hydrogenation plant here to carry out our part of the undertaking. With the change of government in the United States I understand their coal research program was discontinued. There has been criticism of the position taken by the federal government that the pipe line route should be north of the great lakes. But one needs to make no apology for such a policy when the interest of Canadians is being best served. The department which it is my responsibility to administer is well informed as to the prospects and potential markets for gas through northern Ontario. We know that this route with probable sales of gas, offers many advantages in spite of some of the difficulties of terrain and greater distance to markets than a route south of the great lakes.
The acting deputy minister, Dr. Hume, also dealt with this subject in his speech given to the Montreal branch of the Engineering Institute of Canada on February 24 of this year. I quote an extract from Dr. Hume's speech:
Also reference has been repeatedly made to the barren waste of northern Ontario. Anyone familiar with the riches of resources of this area both in mineral and forest products recognizes the value of developments there and the need for fuel. Northern Ontario may well become one of the richest parts of Canada. It has enormous developed and potential resources and it already holds a strategic position in the economic life of this country. To deny it fuel by building the gas pipe line south of the great lakes would be a blow at national unity. This would be advantageous to central Canada as well as New York state because obviously the greatest economies would be achieved by using the whole pipe line to near capacity. Similarly the spill-over into New York state would make possible a very advantageous arrangement for Canada in that gas might be taken on a storage interruptible basis. Delivery need not be made during peak consumption periods provided the volume delivered in off-peak periods fulfils contract specifications on the basis of a stated amount of delivery per year. Such an arrangement need not interfere with large interruptible deliveries to industry in central Canada. Nor need it interfere with storage of gas in off-peak periods to the storage fields of southwestern Ontario where a supply to meet winter peak demands can be maintained.
