speechtext: May I just say one word? I admit there was no understanding that we would sit beyond ten o'clock tonight. I should point out to hon. members that it has been customary in former years to sit extra hours in the closing days of the session. I do not think we have sat beyond ten o'clock more than perhaps four times, and I may be right if I say three times. This is a department in which a great many people are interested, it is true; but we have had, I think, something approaching five hours on it. I am not going to say that is more than average, but certainly it is average and I see no reason why we could not continue tonight in order to dispose of this department. This would leave, I may point out, at least two more days of debate at this rate on what we have left. I think hon. members could perhaps accommodate the rest of the house by continuing at some length tonight rather than calling it ten o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I am quite willing to go on; but so far as accommodation is concerned, I would point out to the minister that on many occasions when members on this side have requested that it be called ten o'clock, at two minutes or three minutes to ten, that request has been denied. I think it is a two-way street. If they desire accommodation we will give it to them, but we would like a little accommodation, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I am sorry if at any time I have not done what I thought hon. members wanted done. I have done my best during the past five or six months to do that. So far as calling it ten o'clock is concerned, I admit that I have asked on four or five occasions, and two or three have been refused. On others, I have not asked and others have refused.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I am not referring to the minister in that respect. It is a general thing that when members on this side would like to call it ten o'clock rather than break into a speech for five minutes, that privilege has been refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Could we all agree that we go on tonight, anyway?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance was not in the committee. While he was out the committee was informed that the minister whose estimates are now before the committee has some information that is very controversial, and he is not in a position to discuss it. I suggest it is now ten minutes after ten and we should report progress and carry on with these estimates now before us the next time we meet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: If it is a question of information that my hon. friend feels could not be given until tomorrow, would it be possible to proceed with some other department for a short time? We have, for example, the supplementary estimates of the department of northern affairs. We have disposed of the department, but there are a few supplementaries and perhaps we could dispose of those?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: If it will please the hon. gentleman I should be pleased to put this on the record, if it is not already on the record. It is a report of our department dealing with the item in which he is interested. I have not read it completely but it is a report issued by our department, and we will stand behind it. I do not know how it compares with what the hon. member for Churchill said or any speech I made in Flin Flon. I do not remember having referred to it during that speech. It seems to be important to my hon. friend, and I shall be very pleased to put it on the record.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
That is the whole point. The hon. member for Churchill put it on the record. He said it meant one thing, and according to my understanding of the English language it means another thing. I said in the house on December 8 that the minister's department did the original research work and made possible the breaking down of this ore. The hon. member for Churchill 50433-428J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys said that was not done here, it was done by the company. The minister, when he was speaking at Flin Flon, was on the side of the hon. member for Churchill and against his own department. Before this item passes I want to read what I said, what the hon. member for Churchill said and what the minister's officials say, and explain to the committee who is right and who is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: This is a report by an engineer, a scientist. The hon. member for Churchill is an engineer, and personally I would not be able to interpret the report and say whose argument is more valid or if there is a conflict between the two statements. I do not think many members in the house would be able to do so. Why not call it a draw? It is not important. The main thing is that a method was found for separating that ore, and this country has benefited from it. I cannot understand why my hon. friend is so sensitive about it. What difference does it make?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The only reason I am sensitive is because I made a statement in the house, in good faith, on information from the minister of the department; and the hon. member for Churchill, for some reason or another, found it necessary to take part in the debate and say that the hon. member for Mackenzie was misinformed and that this work had not been done by the department. Now, all I ask the minister to decide is read what I said and what the hon. member for Churchill said and what his officials said, before this item carries, and make it clear who was right, whether the work was done here or was not done here.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: As I said, I am not a mining engineer and I would not be able to decide which argument is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I am sure the minister has some people in his department who understand the English language. 1 am asking that before this item carries someone who understands the language should read this over and give the minister a statement that he can understand and give to the house. When he spoke in Flin Flon he certainly understood the English language well enough to say that the hon. member for Churchill was right and the hon. member for Mackenzie was wrong. Since there were friends of mine there, they have a right to know whether I was right or wrong, and before this item is carried I am asking the minister to make that clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend has faith in the reports of this department, as we have, then I shall be pleased to put it on the

Supply-Northern Affairs record. It is a report of our department. I shall do that, if it suits his purpose.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: It is now 10.15, and we have spent 15 minutes and have not been able to do anything.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: You spent 15 minutes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I insist that the minister be permitted to read this report and be able to express an opinion before we proceed with the rest of his estimates.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Order. I think perhaps the time has come when I should point out to the committee that hon. members have the right to ask any questions they like, but there comes a time when they cannot insist upon having further answers. Answers given by a minister may be most unsatisfactory, from the point of view of the hon. member asking them, but there does come a time when an hon. member must accept those answers as all he is going to get. I am afraid I cannot let this opportunity pass without making this comment, that when an hon. member says he insists upon getting an answer from a minister before the item is permitted to pass, he always has the alternative to oppose the item.
However, I must draw the attention of the hon. member who has just spoken to the fact that he has had an answer several times, that he may get the same answer again, and that he cannot insist upon getting the answer he wants if the minister does not decide to give it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: You will agree, Mr. Chairman, that I have not asked for this repetition. All I ask is that you call it ten o'clock, which it is my right and privilege to do. I ask you now to call it ten o'clock. It is now 15 minutes after ten.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Before we do that, I said a few moments ago-and my hon. friend did not object to it-that we might proceed to some other items.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: That was ten minutes ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: If I may say so, with respect, the hon. member has been doing all the talking since that time. I understood we were going to take the time to pass other items, if the hon. member really insisted that this item should not pass. That being so, if the committee is agreeable we might proceed to the supplementary estimates on northern affairs and national resources.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Having called the items for this department in the supplementary estimates, and there being no discussion, that completes the supplementary estimates for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. What item does the house leader suggest that we call next?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, while we are waiting, I wonder when it was announced that we were going to take the remainder of the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We were not told on Saturday night that that was proposed for today, and we have not been told during this day that it was to be done. How could hon. members who were particularly interested in these estimates have known that they were coming up? It is most irregular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I announced these on Friday for Saturday; and on Saturday I announced all the remaining estimates for today.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not read that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, then, I must apologize for not having made it clearer on Saturday night. Now, if hon. members would accommodate Mr. Speaker for just a few moments, we could take his estimates under the heading of legislation, and dispose of them. And if hon. members wish to have information as to the proceedings for tomorrow, perhaps I can give it now. We do wish to carry all the other estimates tomorrow, and I would arrange them in any sequence which is convenient. But I think we ought to continue with mines and technical surveys, then take Secretary of State and national revenue, then continue with finance and privy council, and anything there may be left.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be unfair about this matter, but it is easy to make parliament appear ridiculous. I have been here long enough to know that. If we want to run over ten o'clock; if we want to have it understood that we are going to run until two o'clock in the morning, or three or four o'clock, all right; but let us pass a regulation so everybody will know what is going to be done.
It is dangerous to have people think we are going to stop at ten o'clock, and have them go home or be resting, or doing other things they may wish to do, and then go through a lot of estimates we did not expect to be going through. I think that is exceedingly dangerous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I accept my hon. friend's suggestion, for my part, and agree that tomorrow night we will go past ten o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would it not be wise to bring that up tomorrow morning, at the opening of the sitting, so everybody would know?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is the committee of supply, and it would be the committee that would decide to sit beyond ten o'clock tomorrow, unless we completed the work before that time. But I accept my hon. friend's suggestion, as he himself has put it, to have an expeditious disposal of public business.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, I am not just sure where we stand even now. Is there any reason why tomorrow, at the opening of the sitting, we could not introduce a special motion indicating that we would run past ten o'clock, so it would have publicity and everybody would know it would happen? That is the orderly way to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: These things are normally understood, without formal motion. There is no understanding at the moment, but it has been suggested and it will be followed up, and the various parties will be notified.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Did we not pass a resolution some time ago that we would close at ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I say a word. This whole discussion is out of order, because there is nothing before the Chair. But might I suggest this to the members of the committee. Even those who are most faithful, as some are, to the services of the house, still find they are not under the strain that those of us have been who occupy positions at the head of the table. During the last three months of the session we find it impossible to get away even for an hour or two in the evening, let alone ever get out of town.
I think I have noticed in the six years I have been here that by almost implicit consent the usual thing when the end of the session is within, say, a week's sight is that on items which are not greatly contentious we have gone over the ten o'clock hour in order that we might get through. It does not require a regulation; it does not require a motion. All it requires is the unanimous consent of those of us who are left, the faithful members of the house, at the end of the session, to wind up the session and that we think it can best be done by trying to clean up the small matters which are often before the Chair at or about the normal closing time. Now, with the permission of the committee, I shall call legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Order. I find myself in the unfortunate position of being responsible for what goes on in the committee of supply when I am at the head of the table. I am afraid I must point out for the sake of the record that at no time did I see four members, or at any time more than one member, on his feet at one time trying to say something about ten o'clock. There was a discussion as a result of which I think it was quite well understood and quite well agreed that a certain department would be dropped and we would proceed to other items which we have since discussed and passed.
I wish to make this quite clear. There has been no attempt on the part of the chairman this evening, or I think any other evening, to overlook or overrun any member of the house. There has been some difficulty at times in ascertaining the sense of the committee, because when people sit in their seats and call out it is a little hard to decide whether they are saying "go on" or "no" or what. But I was of the opinion that there was unanimous agreement on the part of the committee that we should drop one department and take up another, which we
